A aviação fala em cores: **vermelho**, *: Aviation speaks in colors: **red**, **green**, **yellow**, **amber**, **blue**, **cyan**, **magenta** and **white** appear on displays, aircraft lights and runways. The greatest risk is confusing **red, white and green** signals, and it gets worse in **low light** and with faint colors. In 2002, on a night landing in **Tallahassee**, the first officer's color deficiency on **FedEx 1448** hindered reading the red and white lights of the **PAPI**, the approach slope indicator.
A cabeça se move para olhar atrás das co: The head moves to look behind the windshield posts.
The cabin changes vision in several ways. Even when pressurized, **mild hypoxia** can impair **dark adaptation**, narrow the **visual field**, lower **acuity** and slightly raise the **pressure inside the eye** (See M2V1 - IV). The field can shrink as low as **1,000 to 1,500 m** (about **3,300 to 4,900 ft**); at night, without oxygen, vision can worsen above **5,000 ft**, and smokers feel it sooner.
A cirurgia de **retina** às vezes termin: **Retinal** surgery sometimes ends with a **gas bubble** inside the eye. With the lower cabin pressure, the gas **expands**, eye pressure rises and the person can **lose vision** severely. That is why **no one flies** until the gas is absorbed: about **2 weeks** with **SF6** and **6 weeks** with **C3F8** or **C2F6**. Other surgery inside the eye or a **penetrating injury** to the eye require at least **7 days**. For crew, retinal detachment means unfit until evaluation; the British authority asks for the surgeon's report at a **3-month** review.

A retina tem **três tipos de cone**, mai: The retina has **three types of cone**, most sensitive to **red**, **green** and **blue**; mixing the three gives every color. When one of them is missing or works less, **dyschromatopsia** appears, loosely called color blindness. About **8% of men** and **0.8% of women** fail the strictest tests, and **more than 99%** of them have a **red-green** deficiency. The congenital deficiency passes through the X chromosome and **does not worsen** over time.

A visão noturna é das primeiras funções: Night vision is among the first functions to suffer from **hypoxia** (See M2V1 - IV). Without oxygen, it worsens above **5,000 ft** at night, and **smokers**, with carbon monoxide in the blood, feel it at even lower altitude. In the dark, the **pupil dilates**, the image loses sharpness and the eye tends to focus near, **night myopia**, of up to several diopters.

Na **catarata**, troca-se a lente opaca: In **cataract** surgery, the opaque lens is replaced with an **intraocular lens**. Many people see well the very next day, and the prescription stabilizes in **6 to 8 weeks**. Passengers can fly **24 hours** later. For crew, ICAO considers only the **monofocal** lens suitable; the FAA also accepts lenses for presbyopia, if there is no glare or halos, and applies the same 3-month rule. The British authority keeps the pilot off for **at least 6 weeks**. Months or years later, the capsule may cloud over; the **YAG laser** fixes it in minutes.

No voo, **ver é o primeiro passo** de qu: In flight, **seeing is the first step** of almost every reaction: the pilot perceives, decides and only then acts. The eye has two types of light-sensing cell. **Cones** sit in the center, in the **fovea**, and provide **color** and **detail** in bright light; **rods** sit around them and work in **low light**, without color. Only the fovea sees sharply: just **10°** away from it, acuity already falls to **6/30**, five times worse than normal.

O **ar seco** da cabine resseca e irrita: The cabin's **dry air** dries and irritates the eyes on long flights, and **soft contact lenses** start to bother sooner. The eye does not have trapped air like the ear, with one serious exception: the **gas** the surgeon injects into the eye after retinal surgery **expands** with altitude (See M1V1 - II and M2V4 - VIII).
O **glaucoma** lesa o nervo óptico, em g: **Glaucoma** damages the optic nerve, usually with high **eye pressure**, and starts by taking away pieces of the **visual field** without symptoms. ICAO says to refer anyone with pressure of **24 mmHg** or more, or a difference of **5 mmHg** between the eyes. Under the FAA, the examiner can clear someone with pressure up to **23 mmHg** in both eyes, a **normal visual field** and accepted eye drops; normal-tension glaucoma, secondary glaucoma and filtering surgery go to the FAA for decision.
O **olho seco** piora no ar seco da cabi: **Dry eye** worsens in the cabin's dry air; **preservative-free** artificial tears help, and those with preservatives irritate contact lens wearers. **Conjunctivitis** and **corneal injury** need treatment before flying. A contact lens is a **foreign body**: it can scratch the cornea and cause allergy, ulcers and infection, which is why it needs follow-up.
O **passageiro** pode voar **24 horas**: **Passengers** can fly **24 hours** after corneal laser surgery, if the surgeon clears them. **Crew** wait longer. **ANAC** requires more than **6 months** since surgery and, if requested, normal **glare** and **contrast sensitivity** tests. **ICAO** suggests counting from when the eye drops are stopped: **3 months** with a prescription of up to 6 diopters; between 6 and 10, **3 months** for LASIK and **6** for PRK; above 10, **6 months**. Under the **FAA**, after **3 months**, recovered, with no medication and no symptoms, the case is generally not a concern; before that, only with the eye doctor's report confirming recovery.

O defeito também pode ser **adquirido**,: The deficiency can also be **acquired**, in one eye more than the other and sometimes worsening: diseases of the **retina**, the **optic nerve**, advanced **glaucoma** and medicines such as **hydroxychloroquine**, **ethambutol** and **digitalis**. **Sildenafil**, for erectile dysfunction, makes everything look **bluish** in **3% to 11%** of users for up to 5 hours or more; the FAA requires **8 hours** without flying after it (See M2V4 - VII).
O exame começa com as **placas pseudoiso: The exam starts with **pseudoisochromatic plates**, such as the **Ishihara** plates, viewed in daylight; anyone who fails may take other tests, such as the **D-15** color arrangement, lanterns and the **anomaloscope**. Lenses that "correct" color **do not count**. **ANAC** accepts anyone who reads the plates or, at least, recognizes the basic aviation colors in isolation: **yellow, blue, green, red, white, black and amber**. Under **ICAO**, anyone who fails and cannot distinguish navigation colors and lights is left with a Class 2 **valid by day** only. Under the **FAA**, since **2025** screening is done **once**, on a computer; anyone who fails receives a 3rd class **for day visual flight only**.

O olho vê um **campo** largo, mas nítido: The eye sees a wide **field**, but sharp only in the center. With the gaze fixed, a normal eye reaches about **95°** to the outer side, **60°** toward the nose, **60°** upward and **75°** downward; one eye alone covers about **140°** horizontally. The periphery perceives **motion**, but not detail: to identify an aircraft, you have to bring it onto the **fovea**.

Para o passageiro, a visão de cores **nã: For passengers, color vision **changes nothing**. A crew member with a deficiency flies within the certificate restriction; flying at night or outside it, without clearance, is flying against the rules and against the risk the FedEx case showed. Anyone who notices that colors have **changed** should see an eye doctor, because an acquired deficiency usually has a treatable cause.
Para o tripulante, cada norma tem o seu: For crew, each standard has its own number. At **ANAC**, 1st class requires **20/30 in each eye** and **20/20 with both**, and 2nd class, **20/40** and **20/30**. **ICAO** requires the same: **6/9** and **6/6** for Class 1, and **6/12** and **6/9** for Class 2. The **FAA** requires **20/20 in each eye** for 1st and 2nd class and **20/40** for 3rd. For near vision, all require reading small print at a reading distance; ANAC and ICAO also require the panel distance, at 100 cm, and the FAA, at 80 cm, from age 50.
Para o tripulante, os olhos e as pálpebr: For crew, the eyes and eyelids must work **normally**, with no active disease or after-effect that impairs vision; ANAC also requires normal **visual field**, **eye pressure**, **fundus** and **corneas**. ICAO lists the conditions that make a person **unfit until specialist evaluation**: recurrent keratitis, **keratoconus**, repeated **uveitis**, **retinal detachment**, inflammation of the **optic nerve**, **cataract** that impairs vision, **glaucoma**, nystagmus and **night blindness**. Many are treatable, and the crew member returns afterwards.

A **cinetose**, o enjoo de movimento, su: **Motion sickness** arises when the eyes, the inner ear and the body send messages that do not match: the inner ear feels the turbulence, the eyes see a still cabin. It comes with yawning, pallor, cold sweat, nausea and vomiting. Children under **2 years** rarely get sick; the peak is between **7 and 12 years**. Women are slightly more susceptible, and people with **migraine**, vertigo or inner-ear disease get sick more often.
A **desorientação espacial** é a ideia e: **Spatial disorientation** is the pilot's wrong idea of the aircraft's position, attitude and motion. It is common: many pilots have experienced it, and **5% to 10%** of general aviation accidents are attributed to it, with **90%** of those accidents **fatal**. In questionnaires with more than 3,000 airline pilots, vertigo and disorientation were **4%** of the in-flight incapacitations reported.
The **Coriolis illusion** is the strongest. In a long turn, an abrupt **head** movement, to pick up a chart from the floor or to look back, makes the body feel a rotation about another axis, almost impossible to ignore. That is why, in a turn and in cloud, the head stays **still**.
A **vertigem por cintilação** não vem do: **Flicker vertigo** does not come from the inner ear, but it confuses just the same: a light flashing **4 to 20 times per second**, such as the sun cut by the propeller or the anti-collision light reflecting in cloud, can cause nausea, dizziness and, in sensitive people, loss of consciousness. For passengers, these illusions pose no risk; for pilots, they are a known cause of accidents.
A **vertigem** verdadeira, a sensação de: True **vertigo**, the sensation of spinning, is something else: it comes from inner-ear disease, such as **Ménière's disease**, **vestibular neuritis** and **positional vertigo**, or from pressure, such as **alternobaric vertigo** on descent. For crew, ANAC and ICAO do not accept a permanent vestibular disorder; a transient one grounds until recovery. Waiting times and surgeries are in M2V3 (See M2V3 - III).

A primeira defesa é **conhecer a ilusão*: The first defense is **knowing the illusion**. Feeling on the ground how the inner ear deceives, in a **Bárány chair** or a **disorientation simulator**, teaches you to recognize the conflict when it shows up in flight. ICAO recommends that pilots have an instructor demonstrate the maneuvers that cause disorientation.
A segunda é o **treino por instrumentos*: The second is **instrument training**. The FAA recommends training and maintaining proficiency in controlling the aircraft by instruments **before** flying with less than **3 miles** of visibility. At night and in poor visibility, the instruments are the reference, together with what is seen outside, and they must be tested before takeoff.
A terceira é **planejar**: conferir o te: The third is **planning**: check the weather before departure, en route and at the destination; know the region's geography; do not attempt visual flight when the weather may close in; keep night flying current. Those who fly single-engine IFR often can have a **standby attitude indicator**, so as not to lose the reference in a failure.

Os **otólitos** criam ilusões de arfagem: The **otoliths** create pitch illusions. In the **somatogravic illusion**, the acceleration of a takeoff or go-around without visibility feels like **nose-up**; the pilot pushes the stick and may fly the aircraft into the ground. Reducing power suddenly does the opposite. In **inversion**, leveling off from a climb gives the sensation of tumbling backward; in the **elevator** illusion, an updraft feels like a climb, and the pilot also pushes the nose down.

In the **false horizon**, a sloping cloud layer or ground lights mistaken for stars make the pilot level the aircraft with a line that is not the horizon. In **autokinesis**, a still light, stared at in the dark for many seconds, seems to move; a pilot who tries to follow it may lose control.

In a coordinated turn, the resulting force still points into the seat, and the body feels the aircraft **level**. Without a horizon, in cloud, at night or in haze, the brain starts believing these wrong signals: this is **spatial disorientation**.
Os otólitos não separam gravidade de ace: The otoliths do not separate gravity from acceleration; the pilot feels nose-up and may push the stick toward the ground.
Os remédios funcionam melhor **antes** d: Medications work best **before** the flight. **Scopolamine** lasts about **4 hours** orally and **72 hours** as a patch, and is slightly less sedating; it is not for people with **glaucoma** or risk of urinary retention. **Dimenhydrinate** and **meclizine** cause drowsiness; **promethazine** causes the most. Non-drowsy antihistamines, such as **loratadine**, **fexofenadine** and **cetirizine**, and **ondansetron** **do not work** against motion sickness. In children, any medication calls for caution, and scopolamine should be avoided.
Os sinais de que a desorientação começou: The signs that disorientation has started: the body says one thing and the panel says another; the urge to correct a bank the instruments do not show; altitude or speed changing for no reason; confusion when mixing the outside view with the panel, as **34%** of pilots reported in the FAA survey. A pilot who recognizes the conflict can still overcome it by instruments; one who does not recognize it follows the sensation.

**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Peça **ass: **How to prevent and ease it.** Ask for **assistance** when you buy the ticket: wheelchair, early boarding and a seat near the lavatory, if needed. Carry your medicines in your carry-on bag and keep to the **schedule**, especially with Parkinson's, adjusting to the time zone with your doctor. With multiple sclerosis, carry the neurologist's report listing the medicines you take. With dementia, travel with a **companion** who knows the routine. Crew members do the periodic follow-up the authority requires.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Respeite o: **How to prevent and ease it.** Respect the waiting time and carry the medical report. Ask the airline in advance for **oxygen** if the stroke was less than 2 weeks ago, for a **wheelchair** and early boarding if there is weakness, and travel with a companion. Take your medicines on schedule, including the anticoagulant (See M2V2 - VII), drink water and move your legs. If a new sign appears on board, **tell the crew right away**: the pilot can divert to a hospital.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Tome o ant: **How to prevent and ease it.** Take the anticonvulsant **on schedule**, adjusting to the time zone with your doctor, and carry enough for the whole trip, plus the emergency medicine, in your **carry-on bag**. Sleep before the flight and avoid alcohol. Travel with someone who knows what to do and tell the crew you have epilepsy. Anticonvulsants are **incompatible** with crew duties: anyone who needs them does not fly as a pilot until the authority's waiting period is met.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Use **capa: **How to prevent and ease it.** Wear a **helmet** and a seat belt, in the aircraft too. After any blow with fainting, vomiting, confusion or a worsening headache, seek care before travelling. After skull surgery, board only with the neurosurgeon's **written clearance** and, preferably, with imaging showing there is no air. Crew members tell the examiner about any injury with loss of consciousness, however minor it seems.

Medicines count too: **rescue** medicines are for **occasional** use only, with a waiting time before flying, and several preventives are **prohibited**.
A **enxaqueca** é comum: atinge cerca de: **Migraine** is common: it affects about **17%** of women and **10%** of men. **Without aura**, the pain is usually throbbing, on one side, with light and noise bothersome, nausea and vomiting, and lasts hours or days. **With aura**, minutes before the pain come flashing lights, zigzags, loss of part of the vision, tingling or difficulty speaking. There is also aura **without** pain afterwards.
A **síncope** é a perda rápida da consci: **Syncope** is a rapid loss of consciousness and muscle tone from lack of blood to the whole brain, with spontaneous recovery. It happens to **3%** of the population. The most common is **vasovagal** (reflex) syncope: blood pressure drops, sometimes with a slow heart, and the person goes limp and slumps. **Sudden** syncope, without warning, almost always comes from the **heart** (See M2V2 - IV).
A CAA pede pelo menos 24 horas e o reméd: The CAA asks for at least 24 hours and the emergency medicine at hand; uncontrolled epilepsy requires medical clearance.
A ICAO considera inaceitável um risco de: ICAO considers a risk of sudden incapacitation above 1% per year unacceptable.
A espera em pé no corredor, depois de ho: Standing in the aisle after hours of sitting is a typical moment for fainting.

A vasovagal tem **aviso**: um pródromo d: Vasovagal syncope gives a **warning**: a prodrome of **2 to 5 minutes** with darkening or yellowish vision, nausea, yawning, sweating and pallor. The faint lasts **10 to 15 seconds**, with little confusion. In **10%** of cases there are muscle jerks or loss of urine, which is **not** a seizure. It almost always happens **standing up**, rarely seated and almost never lying down; fear, pain, the sight of blood, heat and time on your feet are the triggers.
A viagem mexe com a rotina, e é aí que o: Travel disrupts routine, and that is when symptoms weigh more: in dementia, short sleep and confinement cause agitation; with Parkinson's and epilepsy, the UK CAA asks for the **medication schedule** to be followed strictly on long trips; and the symptoms that most compromise a crew member's flying are **vertigo** and **double vision**, which ICAO cites in multiple sclerosis. For crew members, hiding a progressive diagnosis from the examiner breaks the rules; for passengers, travelling without asking for help raises the risk of a **fall** while boarding and in the aisle.

Na crise **tônico-clônica**, o corpo enr: In a **tonic-clonic** seizure, the body stiffens for **15 to 20 seconds** and then shakes; it usually all ends within **1 to 2 minutes**, followed by confusion, drowsiness and body aches. In a **complex focal** seizure, the person is unaware for a minute or two, with repetitive movements. A **focal** seizure suggests a lesion in the brain that must be looked for. The **EEG** is normal in up to **40%** of people with epilepsy, so the **history** weighs more than the test.

Nem toda pancada na cabeça machuca o **c: Not every blow to the head injures the **brain**. **Traumatic brain injury** means there was loss or alteration of consciousness, a neurological sign or a lesion on imaging. Severity is measured by **post-traumatic amnesia**, the time until memory works again without gaps: up to **1 hour** is mild, **1 to 24 hours** moderate, **1 to 7 days** severe and longer than that very severe.
No **Parkinson**, os sinais são tremor e: In **Parkinson's**, the signs are resting tremor, **stiffness** and **slowness** of movement, progressing slowly in some and quickly in others. In **multiple sclerosis**, the immune system attacks the myelin of the brain and spinal cord, usually between **20 and 40 years** of age, with relapses and remissions: tingling, weakness, changes in vision, speech or bladder. In **dementia**, the problem is memory and judgment; in **transient global amnesia**, the person loses recent memory for up to **24 hours** and then returns to normal.
No avião, síncope e pré-síncope são a **: On aircraft, syncope and presyncope are the **most common emergency**: **37.4%** of cases in a series of almost 12,000 in-flight emergencies. **Dehydration** from the dry air, **alcohol**, fasting, waiting on your feet in the lavatory queue and standing up quickly after hours of sitting all play a part. The cabin's **mild hypoxia** adds to the other factors (See M2V1).

No voo, a enxaqueca tem vários **gatilho: In flight, migraine has several **triggers** at once: the cabin's relative hypoxia, **short sleep**, **skipped meals**, time zones, **noise**, strong sun, stress and **alcohol**, red wine in particular. ICAO also lists cheese and chocolate. For passengers, known, rare or controlled migraine **is no problem**; the exception is a severe, frequent attack with vomiting and prostration.
No voo, o risco é a crise chegar com **p: In flight, the risk is a seizure arriving with **sleep deprivation**, interrupted sleep or **jet lag**, which lower the threshold. On board, the medical kit rarely has an anticonvulsant, and a long seizure may force a **diversion**. For passengers, the UK CAA asks to wait at least **24 hours** after a seizure; anyone with **uncontrolled** epilepsy or a **new** seizure needs medical clearance, and AsMA advises against flying after a seizure in the **last month**.

O **AVC** é a falta de sangue numa parte: A **stroke** is a lack of blood in part of the brain. In **85%** of cases it is **ischemic**, a blocked vessel; the rest are **hemorrhagic**, a ruptured vessel. A **transient ischemic attack** (TIA) gives the same signs but passes on its own: it is a warning, because about **30%** of people who have a TIA will have a stroke within 5 years. High blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, atrial fibrillation and carotid disease are the risk factors.
O **cérebro** não guarda reserva de oxig: The **brain** keeps no oxygen reserve: it depends on blood every second. That is why it is the first organ to feel the **cabin**. At **8,000 ft**, the saturation of someone at rest falls to around **93%** (See M2V2 - I); a healthy person does not even notice, but the lack of oxygen slows thinking long before it causes symptoms (See M2V1 - IV).

O voo mexe também com os **gatilhos** da: Flying also stirs up the **triggers** of brain diseases. The cabin's relative hypoxia can set off **migraine** in some people; **sleep deprivation**, interrupted sleep and **time zones** lower the **seizure** threshold; skipped meals and noise worsen headache; **standing** for a long time, in the heat and with little water, favors **fainting**.
Os sinais chegam **de repente**: **rosto: The signs come **suddenly**: a **drooping face** on one side, an **arm that drifts down** when the person raises both, **slurred or nonsensical speech**, loss of vision, loss of balance, confusion or a sudden, severe headache. Every minute counts, and **there is no thrombolysis on board**, the medicine that unblocks the vessel. On aircraft, stroke is rare, but it is among the emergencies most likely to lead to **diversion** and hospital admission.

Para o passageiro, o prazo depende da gr: For passengers, the waiting time depends on severity. Under **IATA** criteria, a stroke is not accepted up to **day 4**; from **day 5 to day 14**, only if stable with a nurse escort, and with **oxygen** in the first two weeks. The UK **CAA** advises waiting **2 weeks**, and AsMA mentions **2 to 4 weeks** of observation. Anyone with weakness, stiffness, poor balance or slowness needs a **wheelchair**, early boarding and an accessible seat; anyone with urinary urgency, a seat near the **lavatory**. In dementia, the unfamiliar setting, broken routine, short sleep and confinement can bring **agitation**: a companion is recommended.

Para o tripulante, a **ANAC** não aceita: For crew members, **ANAC** does not accept brain surgery or injury with **sequelae** that affect duties. The **FAA** always defers to itself: mild concussion, **6 months**; moderate injury, **12 months**; severe injury, with blood in the brain or amnesia longer than 24 hours, **5 years**. **ICAO** observes for **3 to 6 months** in post-concussion syndrome, **1 to 2 years** for a simple epidural hematoma, **2 years** for subdural and intracerebral hematoma, and up to **5 years** in severe cases. The first step is **conversation**: build rapport, try to calm the person and ask about the diagnosis, the medicines, the last dose and whether they are on board. Then look for another cause: **alcohol and drugs**, intoxication or withdrawal, vital signs and breathing, with water and oxygen if needed.

The **insulin pump** feels the pressure. On the climb, cabin pressure falls, bubbles grow in the reservoir and the pump delivers extra insulin, about **1 to 1.4 units**; on the descent, it draws back and delivers almost 1 unit less. The authors suggest disconnecting the pump before take-off, removing the bubbles and reconnecting at **cruise**; after landing, disconnecting again and priming the tubing with **2 units**. Agree with your doctor before changing how you use it.
A **insulina** vai na **bagagem de mão**: **Insulin** goes in your **carry-on**, never only in checked luggage: the hold can get cold enough to **freeze** insulin, and the bag can get lost. Carry **extra** insulin, split between **two bags**, ideally one with a travel companion, in a **cool bag**. During the flight, it does not need a fridge. Carry your doctor's letter and an ID stating that you use insulin.
The **thyroid** is the body's accelerator. In **hypothyroidism**, it works slowly: tiredness, sleepiness, feeling cold, weight gain, slow thinking. In **hyperthyroidism**, it speeds up: racing heart, tremor, anxiety, feeling hot and weight loss, sometimes with arrhythmia (See M2V2 - IV). In **Graves' disease**, the eyes may bulge and **double vision** may appear (See M2V4 - VII).

No **diabetes**, o açúcar do sangue fica: In **diabetes**, blood sugar is high because insulin is lacking (**type 1**) or because the body responds poorly to it (**type 2**). For flying, the greatest danger is not high sugar but **low sugar**, **hypoglycaemia**: tremor, sweating, hunger, confusion and, if nothing is done, fainting and even coma. It is a **sudden incapacitation**. Very high sugar also gets in the way: blurred vision, tiredness and slow thinking.
No **hipertireoidismo**, o remédio antit: In **hyperthyroidism**, an antithyroid drug without side effects does not disqualify, but the pilot is unfit until function returns to normal, and for 1st class the ophthalmologist checks **eye movements** and double vision. After **surgery** or **radioactive iodine**, grounding lasts until the end of treatment and stable function, with a blood test every year. ANAC assesses significant over- or underfunction and the effects of replacement hormone case by case.

A **diarreia** elimina água e sais pelas:
**Diarrhea** causes the loss of water and salts through the stool; it can be caused by infection, medication or inflammation. **Irritable bowel syndrome** causes pain and changes in bowel habits without the destructive inflammation characteristic of **Crohn's disease** and **ulcerative colitis**.

In the cabin, urgency to evacuate and limited access to the bathroom can compromise tasks. **Intense diarrhea** causes dehydration: less blood volume causes weakness, dizziness and a drop in blood pressure. **Blood in the stool**, fever and severe pain suggest a complication that should not be treated as mere travel discomfort.

**Passenger** with mild, tolerable symptoms and without fever or significant dehydration can travel if they are able to keep fluids; a serious crisis requires assessment before embarking. For the **crew member**, stable inflammatory disease may be compatible with fitness after evaluation: the FAA provides criteria for colitis and the European standard requires stable remission in the 1st class, without systemic corticosteroids for control.

An exacerbation with pain, bleeding or disabling diarrhea can suddenly remove the crew member from duty. At the FAA, following a special authorization for colitis requires reevaluation when the disease worsens, requires surgery or requires certain medications; operating during an exacerbation is contrary to the fitness requirement.

**Oral rehydration solution** replaces water and electrolytes in significant losses. **Loperamide** can relieve non-bloody diarrhea, but should not be used alone if there is **fever or blood in the stool**. Antibiotics are not routine prevention; treatment of infections, corticosteroids and immunosuppressants requires a medical plan. For crew members, the effects and underlying illness need assessment.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Before traveling, have safe water, tolerated food and prescribed medicines in your carry-on luggage. Replace losses and avoid boarding with dehydration, fever, blood in the stool or incapacitating crisis. The crew member must leave during exacerbations and return after evaluating clinical control and treatment.
A **vesícula biliar** guarda a bile prod:
The **gallbladder** stores the bile produced by the liver. **Gallstones** can remain silent or block the flow of bile, producing colic, inflammation and jaundice. The **pancreas** releases digestive enzymes; when it becomes inflamed, **pancreatitis** can cause intense pain, vomiting and systemic illness.

An attack of biliary colic or pancreatitis is not just a stomach ache. **Obstruction**, inflammation and vomiting can progress without adequate assistance during the flight. Expansion of gas in the intestine can add distension, but is not the cause of stones or pancreatitis.

**Passengers** with asymptomatic stones and no complications can receive medical advice to travel; persistent pain, fever, jaundice with malaise and significant vomiting require prior evaluation. **Crew** requires individual aeromedical decision: in European standards, symptomatic stones and active pancreatitis prevent fitness; asymptomatic stone can be considered after assessment according to class and context.

A sudden crisis may disable you from commanding or serving in the cabin. The FAA has separate provisions for stones and pancreatitis; ANAC assesses the risk of digestive incapacitation. Returning after pain has improved without clarifying the cause is not enough to confirm fitness.

Analgesics and antispasmodics can hide the worsening or cause drowsiness; after gallbladder surgery, the abdominal procedure recovery criteria also apply. **Antibiotics**, surgery or other treatments should be guided by the cause, not an improvised pre-flight dose.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Differentiate the presence of stones without symptoms from a recent episode of obstruction, fever, severe pain or pancreatitis. Take the report and therapeutic plan, avoid foods that trigger pain individually and don't embark on a crisis. The crew member returns only when the cause is controlled, without disabling effects and after aeromedical evaluation.

O **estômago** recebe e mistura o alimen:
The **stomach** receives and mixes the food; the **intestine** absorbs water and nutrients; the **liver** processes substances, produces bile and participates in clotting. Flight does not interrupt these functions, but it can transform a controlled problem into an emergency when there is pain, vomiting, bleeding or obstruction.

During ascent, **cabin pressure decreases** and the air trapped in the stomach and intestine **expands**. This can cause distension, cramping and increased tension over a fresh abdominal suture (See M1V1 - II). The effect is especially dangerous if there is already an obstruction, because the gas cannot advance.

There is **less oxygen** than at sea level in the pressurized cabin. A person with digestive bleeding, anemia or advanced liver disease may tolerate this reduction worse, because the blood carries less oxygen or the body has less reserve (See M2V1 - I). Do not attribute dizziness accompanied by blood in the stool to a simple indisposition.

**Dry air**, **immobility**, changing meals and **time zone** favor discomfort, constipation or dehydration when there is already loss of fluids due to diarrhea or vomiting (See M1V1 - IV; see M2V8 - III). Intense G-forces are not a common factor in the passenger cabin; in aerobatic aviation, sudden pain can impair the crew member's performance.

Passengers and crew need to distinguish between **mild discomfort** and **acute abdomen**. Intense progressive pain, stiff belly, persistent vomiting, vomited blood, black stools with malaise or fainting require urgent evaluation, not an attempt to treat the symptom already on board.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Before traveling, treat active symptoms and discuss recent surgeries, decompensated liver disease or intestinal crises with your doctor. Choose food that is already tolerated and take medicines in your hand luggage. During the flight, hydrate according to your clinical condition and move when allowed; the crew member with disabling symptoms must suspend the activity and seek evaluation.
O **fígado** produz proteínas da coagula:
The **liver** produces clotting proteins, transforms medications and helps eliminate substances. **Hepatitis** is liver inflammation; **liver disease associated with metabolic dysfunction** can progress to scarring; **cirrhosis** is an advanced lesion that compromises circulation and organ function.

Cirrhosis can cause **ascites** (fluid in the abdomen), **varices in the esophagus** and **hepatic encephalopathy**, when substances that the liver cannot clear harm the brain. Distension due to cabin gas adds discomfort to ascites; bleeding, confusion and weakness can become in-flight emergencies.

A person with an isolated laboratory abnormality or stable liver disease does not automatically receive a travel ban: the doctor needs to assess function, symptoms and complications. **Digestive bleeding, new confusion, significant jaundice with malaise or decompensated ascites** require evaluation before boarding. The **FAA** allows decision by the examiner in resolved hepatitis without sequelae and requires individual analysis of active liver diseases.

For **crew members**, ANAC requires the absence of digestive impairment that could incapacitate; european standards allow liver function to be assessed after a satisfactory gastroenterological report, but **esophageal varices** are considered incompatible with fitness in the aforementioned European guidelines. Hiding confusion, bleeding or medication effects puts the operation at risk.

**Diuretics** can help control ascites, but also reduce volume and electrolytes; **lactulose** can increase bowel movements; certain sedatives worsen attention and encephalopathy. The prescription must consider hepatic metabolism and safety of function; none of these remedies, in isolation, authorizes a crew member to fly.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Before traveling, confirm liver stability, absence of bleeding and plan for medications, food and fluids. Avoid alcohol and self-medication. In the cabin, follow your individual hydration plan, as ascites and diuretics may require different restrictions. If there is abnormal drowsiness, confusion, vomited blood or black stools, do not board or operate.

No **refluxo gastroesofágico**, o conteú:
In **gastroesophageal reflux**, the acidic contents of the stomach return to the esophagus and cause burning or regurgitation. **Gastritis** is inflammation of the stomach lining; a **peptic ulcer** is a lesion that can bleed or perforate. Reflux and gastritis are not synonymous with ulcers.

Irregular meal times, lying down soon after eating and **expanding gas** can increase burping and the feeling of a full stomach. An active ulcer deserves special attention: sudden severe pain, vomiting with blood or black stools can announce **perforation** or **hemorrhage**, with a drop in pressure and loss of consciousness.

A **passenger** with mild, controlled heartburn and no warning signs can usually travel with care. If there is a bleeding ulcer, perforation, severe pain or repeated vomiting, **do not board** before assessment and stabilization. The **crew member** must be without risk of incapacitation; the ANAC evaluates the digestive requirement and the FAA uses its own provisions for reflux and ulcers, without automatic release through the simple use of treatment.

Flying with omitted active disease can turn severe bleeding or pain into an emergency where no endoscopy or surgery is available. For the crew member, the condition that impairs fitness must be communicated to the examiner; continuing to operate without conditions may affect certification and operational safety.

**Proton pump inhibitors** and other acidity reducers can control symptoms, but the medicine does not show that the ulcer has healed. **Anti-inflammatories**, alcohol and self-medication can aggravate injuries and bleeding; sedative analgesics impair attention and judgment. The doctor must identify the cause, treat and confirm recovery when indicated.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Eat smaller portions, avoid foods that already cause symptoms and don't lie down right after meals. Take prescribed medication and do not start sedative treatment before a stopover. Passengers with bleeding, severe pain or persistent vomiting must postpone the flight; the crew member needs the relevant aeromedical assessment before resuming.
Depois de **cirurgia abdominal**, o inte:
After **abdominal surgery**, the intestine may temporarily slow down and accumulate air. The decrease in cabin pressure causes the gas to **increase in volume**, pulling tissue and, post-operatively, potentially threatening sutures and anastomoses. This can lead to **pain, bleeding or perforation** (See M1V1 - II).

For the **passenger**, one UK CAA guideline recommends **avoiding air travel for 10 days after abdominal surgery**, while another UK CAA publication allows shorter intervals after uncomplicated minor procedures. The actual timing depends on the operation, clinical recovery and the surgeon's assessment. After **colonoscopy with the introduction of a large volume of gas**, it is recommended **24 hours** without flying. After **laparoscopy**, the reference mentions around **24 hours** for residual gas, but this interval **is not equivalent to surgical release from a major operation**: the risk of the wound and the disease operated on may require additional waiting.

The **crew member** is assessed for physical capacity, repair integrity and risk of incapacitation, with different intervals in British guidance: around **1 week** after diagnostic-only laparoscopy; **3 to 4 weeks** after major laparoscopic procedures such as cholecystectomy or inguinal hernia; **2 to 3 months** after major abdominal surgery, such as colectomy. These are reference ranges for fitness consideration, not automatic release. After lower gastrointestinal endoscopy with **biopsy or polypectomy**, the British pilot guidance is **at least 48 hours** and communication to the examiner.

At **ANAC**, RBAC 67 requires that major digestive surgery, flow diversion or sequelae with the possibility of incapacitation be evaluated by the examiner or authority. **Hernias** capable of causing pain or trapping intestinal loops are also included in the evaluation: an **obstruction** retains gas and liquids, distends the intestine and can worsen during ascent. **ICAO** and **EASA** also require satisfactory recovery and minimal risk of complications. For both profiles, progressive pain, fever, worsening distension, persistent vomiting or bleeding are reasons to **not fly**.

Flying before healing or hiding a complication prevents a quick response if there is a perforation or hemorrhage. Analgesics with sedative effects decrease alertness and evacuation capacity; pain medication is not a substitute for post-operative review. The final decision depends on the type of intervention, physical examination and surgeon's guidance; for crew members, also for the aeromedical examiner.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Before boarding, take a summary of the surgery, confirm intestinal function, healing, absence of relevant pain and ability to walk and sit safely. Do not use the shorter timeframe of a colonoscopy to justify travel after surgery. Crew members must complete the aeromedical reassessment and not return with pain, weakness or sedative medication.
A **vesícula biliar** guarda a bile prod:
The **gallbladder** stores the bile produced by the liver. **Gallstones** can remain silent or block the flow of bile, producing colic, inflammation and jaundice. The **pancreas** releases digestive enzymes; when it becomes inflamed, **pancreatitis** can cause intense pain, vomiting and systemic illness.

An attack of biliary colic or pancreatitis is not just a stomach ache. **Obstruction**, inflammation and vomiting can progress without adequate assistance during the flight. Expansion of gas in the intestine can add distension, but is not the cause of stones or pancreatitis.

**Passengers** with asymptomatic stones and no complications can receive medical advice to travel; persistent pain, fever, jaundice with malaise and significant vomiting require prior evaluation. **Crew** requires individual aeromedical decision: in European standards, symptomatic stones and active pancreatitis prevent fitness; asymptomatic stone can be considered after assessment according to class and context.

A sudden crisis may incapacitate the crew member in command or during cabin service. The FAA has separate provisions for stones and pancreatitis; ANAC assesses the risk of digestive incapacitation. Returning after pain has improved without clarifying the cause is not enough to confirm fitness.

Analgesics and antispasmodics can hide the worsening or cause drowsiness; after gallbladder surgery, the abdominal procedure recovery criteria also apply. **Antibiotics**, surgery or other treatments should be guided by the cause, not an improvised pre-flight dose.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Differentiate the presence of stones without symptoms from a recent episode of obstruction, fever, severe pain or pancreatitis. Take the report and therapeutic plan, avoid foods that trigger pain individually and don't embark on a crisis. The crew member returns only when the cause is controlled, without disabling effects and after aeromedical evaluation.

O **estômago** recebe e mistura o alimen:
The **stomach** receives and mixes the food; the **intestine** absorbs water and nutrients; the **liver** processes substances, produces bile and participates in clotting. Flight does not interrupt these functions, but it can transform a controlled problem into an emergency when there is pain, vomiting, bleeding or obstruction.

During ascent, **cabin pressure decreases** and the air trapped in the stomach and intestine **expands**. This can cause distension, cramping and increased tension over a fresh abdominal suture (See M1V1 - II). The effect is especially dangerous if there is already an obstruction, because the gas cannot advance.

There is **less oxygen** than at sea level in the pressurized cabin. A person with digestive bleeding, anemia or advanced liver disease may tolerate this reduction worse, because the blood carries less oxygen or the body has less reserve (See M2V1 - I). Do not attribute dizziness accompanied by blood in the stool to a simple indisposition.

**Dry air**, **immobility**, changing meals and **time zone** favor discomfort, constipation or dehydration when there is already loss of fluids due to diarrhea or vomiting (See M1V1 - IV and M2V8 - III). Intense G-forces are not a common factor in the passenger cabin; in aerobatic aviation, sudden pain can impair the crew member's performance.

Passengers and crew need to distinguish between **mild discomfort** and **acute abdomen**. Intense progressive pain, stiff belly, persistent vomiting, vomited blood, black stools with malaise or fainting require urgent evaluation, not an attempt to treat the symptom already on board.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Before traveling, treat active symptoms and discuss recent surgeries, decompensated liver disease or intestinal crises with your doctor. Choose food that is already tolerated and take medicines in your hand luggage. During the flight, hydrate according to your clinical condition and move when allowed; the crew member with disabling symptoms must suspend the activity and seek evaluation.

O **estômago** recebe e mistura o alimen: The **stomach** receives and mixes the food; the **intestine** absorbs water and nutrients; the **liver** processes substances, produces bile and participates in clotting. Flight does not interrupt these functions, but it can transform a controlled problem into an emergency when there is pain, vomiting, bleeding or obstruction.
Na subida, a **pressão da cabine diminui: During ascent, **cabin pressure decreases** and the air trapped in the stomach and intestine **expands**. This can cause distension, cramping and increased tension over a fresh abdominal suture (See M1V1 - II). The effect is especially dangerous if there is already an obstruction, because the gas cannot advance.
Há **menos oxigênio** do que ao nível do: There is **less oxygen** than at sea level in the pressurized cabin. A person with digestive bleeding, anemia or advanced liver disease may tolerate this reduction worse, because the blood carries less oxygen or the body has less reserve (See M2V1 - I). Do not attribute dizziness accompanied by blood in the stool to a simple indisposition.
O **ar seco**, a **imobilidade**, a muda: **Dry air**, **immobility**, changing meals and **time zone** favor discomfort, constipation or dehydration when there is already loss of fluids due to diarrhea or vomiting (See M1V1 - IV and M2V8 - III). Intense G-forces are not a common factor in the passenger cabin; in aerobatic aviation, sudden pain can impair the crew member's performance.
Passageiro e tripulante precisam disting: Passengers and crew need to distinguish between **mild discomfort** and **acute abdomen**. Intense progressive pain, stiff belly, persistent vomiting, vomited blood, black stools with malaise or fainting require urgent evaluation, not an attempt to treat the symptom already on board.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes de v: **How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Before traveling, treat active symptoms and discuss recent surgeries, decompensated liver disease or intestinal crises with your doctor. Choose food that is already tolerated and take medicines in your hand luggage. During the flight, hydrate according to your clinical condition and move when allowed; the crew member with disabling symptoms must suspend the activity and seek evaluation.
No **refluxo gastroesofágico**, o conteú: In **gastroesophageal reflux**, the acidic contents of the stomach return to the esophagus and cause burning or regurgitation. **Gastritis** is inflammation of the stomach lining; a **peptic ulcer** is a lesion that can bleed or perforate. Reflux and gastritis are not synonymous with ulcers.
Refeições fora de hora, deitar-se logo a: Irregular meal times, lying down soon after eating and **expanding gas** can increase burping and the feeling of a full stomach. An active ulcer deserves special attention: sudden severe pain, vomiting with blood or black stools can announce **perforation** or **hemorrhage**, with a drop in pressure and loss of consciousness.
O **passageiro** com azia leve, controla: A **passenger** with mild, controlled heartburn and no warning signs can usually travel with care. If there is a bleeding ulcer, perforation, severe pain or repeated vomiting, **do not board** before assessment and stabilization. The **crew member** must be without risk of incapacitation; the ANAC evaluates the digestive requirement and the FAA uses its own provisions for reflux and ulcers, without automatic release through the simple use of treatment.
Voar com doença ativa omitida pode trans: Flying with omitted active disease can turn severe bleeding or pain into an emergency where no endoscopy or surgery is available. For the crew member, the condition that impairs fitness must be communicated to the examiner; continuing to operate without conditions may affect certification and operational safety.
**Inibidores da bomba de prótons** e out: **Proton pump inhibitors** and other acidity reducers can control symptoms, but the medicine does not show that the ulcer has healed. **Anti-inflammatories**, alcohol and self-medication can aggravate injuries and bleeding; sedative analgesics impair attention and judgment. The doctor must identify the cause, treat and confirm recovery when indicated.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Coma porçõ: **How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Eat smaller portions, avoid foods that already cause symptoms and don't lie down right after meals. Take prescribed medication and do not start sedative treatment before a stopover. Passengers with bleeding, severe pain or persistent vomiting must postpone the flight; the crew member needs the relevant aeromedical assessment before resuming.
A **diarreia** elimina água e sais pelas: **Diarrhea** causes the loss of water and salts through the stool; it can be caused by infection, medication or inflammation. **Irritable bowel syndrome** causes pain and changes in bowel habits without the destructive inflammation characteristic of **Crohn's disease** and **ulcerative colitis**.
Na cabine, urgência para evacuar e acess: In the cabin, urgency to evacuate and limited access to the bathroom can compromise tasks. **Intense diarrhea** causes dehydration: less blood volume causes weakness, dizziness and a drop in blood pressure. **Blood in the stool**, fever and severe pain suggest a complication that should not be treated as mere travel discomfort.
O **passageiro** com sintomas leves, tol: **Passenger** with mild, tolerable symptoms and without fever or significant dehydration can travel if they are able to keep fluids; a serious crisis requires assessment before embarking. For the **crew member**, stable inflammatory disease may be compatible with fitness after evaluation: the FAA provides criteria for colitis and the European standard requires stable remission in the 1st class, without systemic corticosteroids for control.
Uma exacerbação com dor, sangramento ou: An exacerbation with pain, bleeding or disabling diarrhea can suddenly remove the crew member from duty. At the FAA, following a special authorization for colitis requires reevaluation when the disease worsens, requires surgery or requires certain medications; operating during an exacerbation is contrary to the fitness requirement.
**Solução de reidratação oral** repõe ág: **Oral rehydration solution** replaces water and electrolytes in significant losses. **Loperamide** can relieve non-bloody diarrhea, but should not be used alone if there is **fever or blood in the stool**. Antibiotics are not routine prevention; treatment of infections, corticosteroids and immunosuppressants requires a medical plan. For crew members, the effects and underlying illness need assessment.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes da v: **How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Before traveling, have safe water, tolerated food and prescribed medicines in your carry-on luggage. Replace losses and avoid boarding with dehydration, fever, blood in the stool or incapacitating crisis. The crew member must leave during exacerbations and return after evaluating clinical control and treatment.
O **fígado** produz proteínas da coagula: The **liver** produces clotting proteins, transforms medications and helps eliminate substances. **Hepatitis** is liver inflammation; **liver disease associated with metabolic dysfunction** can progress to scarring; **cirrhosis** is an advanced lesion that compromises circulation and organ function.
A cirrose pode provocar **ascite** (líqu: Cirrhosis can cause **ascites** (fluid in the abdomen), **varices in the esophagus** and **hepatic encephalopathy**, when substances that the liver cannot clear harm the brain. Distension due to cabin gas adds discomfort to ascites; bleeding, confusion and weakness can become in-flight emergencies.
Uma pessoa com alteração laboratorial is: A person with an isolated laboratory abnormality or stable liver disease does not automatically receive a travel ban: the doctor needs to assess function, symptoms and complications. **Digestive bleeding, new confusion, significant jaundice with malaise or decompensated ascites** require evaluation before boarding. The **FAA** allows decision by the examiner in resolved hepatitis without sequelae and requires individual analysis of active liver diseases.
Para **tripulantes**, a ANAC exige ausên: For **crew members**, ANAC requires the absence of digestive impairment that could incapacitate; european standards allow liver function to be assessed after a satisfactory gastroenterological report, but **esophageal varices** are considered incompatible with fitness in the aforementioned European guidelines. Hiding confusion, bleeding or medication effects puts the operation at risk.
**Diuréticos** podem ajudar a controlar: **Diuretics** can help control ascites, but also reduce volume and electrolytes; **lactulose** can increase bowel movements; certain sedatives worsen attention and encephalopathy. The prescription must consider hepatic metabolism and safety of function; none of these remedies, in isolation, authorizes a crew member to fly.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes da v: **How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Before traveling, confirm liver stability, absence of bleeding and plan for medications, food and fluids. Avoid alcohol and self-medication. In the cabin, follow your individual hydration plan, as ascites and diuretics may require different restrictions. If there is abnormal drowsiness, confusion, vomited blood or black stools, do not board or operate.
A **vesícula biliar** guarda a bile prod: The **gallbladder** stores the bile produced by the liver. **Gallstones** can remain silent or block the flow of bile, producing colic, inflammation and jaundice. The **pancreas** releases digestive enzymes; when it becomes inflamed, **pancreatitis** can cause intense pain, vomiting and systemic illness.
Uma crise de cólica biliar ou pancreatit: An attack of biliary colic or pancreatitis is not just a stomach ache. **Obstruction**, inflammation and vomiting can progress without adequate assistance during the flight. Expansion of gas in the intestine can add distension, but is not the cause of stones or pancreatitis.
**Passageiros** com cálculo assintomátic: **Passengers** with asymptomatic stones and no complications can receive medical advice to travel; persistent pain, fever, jaundice with malaise and significant vomiting require prior evaluation. **Crew** requires individual aeromedical decision: in European standards, symptomatic stones and active pancreatitis prevent fitness; asymptomatic stone can be considered after assessment according to class and context.
Uma crise súbita pode incapacitar o trip: A sudden crisis may incapacitate the crew member in command or during cabin service. The FAA has separate provisions for stones and pancreatitis; ANAC assesses the risk of digestive incapacitation. Returning after pain has improved without clarifying the cause is not enough to confirm fitness.
Analgésicos e antiespasmódicos podem esc: Analgesics and antispasmodics can hide the worsening or cause drowsiness; after gallbladder surgery, the abdominal procedure recovery criteria also apply. **Antibiotics**, surgery or other treatments should be guided by the cause, not an improvised pre-flight dose.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Diferencie: **How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Differentiate the presence of stones without symptoms from a recent episode of obstruction, fever, severe pain or pancreatitis. Take the report and therapeutic plan, avoid foods that trigger pain individually and don't embark on a crisis. The crew member returns only when the cause is controlled, without disabling effects and after aeromedical evaluation.
Depois de **cirurgia abdominal**, o inte: After **abdominal surgery**, the intestine may temporarily slow down and accumulate air. The decrease in cabin pressure causes the gas to **increase in volume**, pulling tissue and, post-operatively, potentially threatening sutures and anastomoses. This can lead to **pain, bleeding or perforation** (See M1V1 - II).
Para o **passageiro**, uma orientação es: For the **passenger**, one UK CAA guideline recommends **avoiding air travel for 10 days after abdominal surgery**, while another UK CAA publication allows shorter intervals after uncomplicated minor procedures. The actual timing depends on the operation, clinical recovery and the surgeon's assessment. After **colonoscopy with the introduction of a large volume of gas**, it is recommended **24 hours** without flying. After **laparoscopy**, the reference mentions around **24 hours** for residual gas, but this interval **is not equivalent to surgical release from a major operation**: the risk of the wound and the disease operated on may require additional waiting.
O **tripulante** é avaliado por capacida: The **crew member** is assessed for physical capacity, repair integrity and risk of incapacitation, with different intervals in British guidance: around **1 week** after diagnostic-only laparoscopy; **3 to 4 weeks** after major laparoscopic procedures such as cholecystectomy or inguinal hernia; **2 to 3 months** after major abdominal surgery, such as colectomy. These are reference ranges for fitness consideration, not automatic release. After lower gastrointestinal endoscopy with **biopsy or polypectomy**, the British pilot guidance is **at least 48 hours** and communication to the examiner.
Na **ANAC**, o RBAC 67 exige que cirurgi: At **ANAC**, RBAC 67 requires that major digestive surgery, flow diversion or sequelae with the possibility of incapacitation be evaluated by the examiner or authority. **Hernias** capable of causing pain or trapping intestinal loops are also included in the evaluation: an **obstruction** retains gas and liquids, distends the intestine and can worsen during ascent. **ICAO** and **EASA** also require satisfactory recovery and minimal risk of complications. For both profiles, progressive pain, fever, worsening distension, persistent vomiting or bleeding are reasons to **not fly**.
Voar antes da cicatrização ou esconder u: Flying before healing or hiding a complication prevents a quick response if there is a perforation or hemorrhage. Analgesics with sedative effects decrease alertness and evacuation capacity; pain medication is not a substitute for post-operative review. The final decision depends on the type of intervention, physical examination and surgeon's guidance; for crew members, also for the aeromedical examiner.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes de e: **How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Before boarding, take a summary of the surgery, confirm intestinal function, healing, absence of relevant pain and ability to walk and sit safely. Do not use the shorter timeframe of a colonoscopy to justify travel after surgery. Crew members must complete the aeromedical reassessment and not return with pain, weakness or sedative medication.
**Câncer** reúne doenças de crescimento:
**Cancer** brings together diseases of unregulated cell growth, with very different consequences depending on the organ, stage and treatment. A patient being followed up after curative treatment does not present the same risk as someone with active neoplasia and complications. Flight does not transform a stable lesion into metastasis; the main concerns include anemia, pain, functional loss, infection, bleeding, thrombosis, lung changes, and effects of surgery or chemotherapy.

In the cabin, the reduction in available oxygen can accentuate symptoms of **anemia or pulmonary impairment**. Active cancer and certain treatments can increase the thrombotic tendency, while thrombocytopenia favors bleeding. Immobility and dehydration increase existing vulnerabilities. If the tumor obstructs the airways, compromises breathing or affects the nervous system, it is the **functional reserve** — and not the diagnosis alone — that determines the immediate risk. (See M2V1 and M2V2.)

**For the passenger**, the decision considers blood count, infection, disease activity, recent treatment, need for support and access to care at the destination. The CDC recommends postponing travel in the face of major bleeding or severe immunosuppression, anemia, or thrombocytopenia. **For the crew member**, active disease, disabling therapies and possible cognitive effects require aeromedical investigation and evaluation; The standards of the competent authority and the type of neoplasm determine the certification path.

Traveling without assessment during **febrile neutropenia**, bleeding, persistent vomiting or disabling pain may result in an onboard emergency and delayed treatment. Fever in a patient undergoing chemotherapy requires rapid medical evaluation: it may be the only sign of a serious infection. A pulmonary thrombosis or embolism can cause sudden shortness of breath, and recent surgical interventions require special consideration. Discharge from hospital, absence of pain and healthy appearance do not replace risk analysis.

**Chemotherapy, targeted therapies, immunotherapy, corticosteroids and supportive medications** have different toxicity and interaction profiles. Nausea, fatigue, neuropathy, diarrhea and drowsiness may reduce traveling or operating safety. Vaccination during immunosuppression requires specific assessment, and live vaccines may be contraindicated. Never rearrange chemotherapy cycles, suspend prophylactic anticoagulation or start preventive medication without the oncologist's agreement.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Plan the trip with the oncologist and bring a report, recent blood count when indicated and information about complications and medications. Assess risk of thrombosis and support before long flights; maintain a mask and hygiene when protection against infections is indicated. Postpone in the presence of fever, bleeding, new dyspnea or inability to eat and hydrate. The professional must also check assistance at the destination, insurance and possible need for MEDIF.
**Doenças transmissíveis** podem alcança:
**Communicable diseases** can reach other people through respiratory particles, contact, blood, food or vectors, depending on the agent. The mere presence of an infection does not imply airborne contagiousness. In air transport, close coexistence and exposure time matter, but the risk depends on the route of transmission, the stage of the disease and control measures. Separating these situations protects passengers without stigmatizing those living with a chronic condition.

The cabin has ventilation and filtration systems that help dilute particles, but **do not eliminate all exposures**, especially when someone symptomatic is nearby. Fever, intense cough, dyspnea and dehydration also compromise your health while traveling. People with immunosuppression, lung disease or advanced age may suffer a more severe outcome because they have less reserve or defense. Measures against respiratory contamination do not replace precautions for diseases transmitted by blood, food or vectors.

**Passengers** with an acute communicable disease must consult health recommendations and postpone the trip when there is a relevant risk of transmission or clinical incapacity. There is no single deadline applicable to influenza, COVID-19, tuberculosis, meningitis or other infections. **The crew member** must not work with incapacitating fever, symptoms that affect attention or illness that compromises performance; return requires stability and compliance with applicable health and aeromedical rules.

Flying with **shortness of breath, hypoxemia, intense prostration or persistent fever** can aggravate the condition and make timely care difficult. Contagious people can generate transmission on board or at destination, even without prolonged contact with all occupants. Infectious pulmonary tuberculosis, severe respiratory infection or suspected notifiable disease require coordination with health services; the traveler should not use other people's absence of symptoms as proof of safety.

**Antibiotics, antivirals and antipyretics** treat specific indications; No medication is automatically authorized to board. The effect of infection, the interaction between drugs and adverse reactions need to be evaluated, especially for those who operate aircraft. Appropriate masks, hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette and ventilation are complementary measures when indicated. The prescription should not be started or stopped to simply hide a fever and overcome a screening.

**How ​​to prevent and mitigate.** Before your flight, check symptoms, local guidelines and public health recommendations for the destination. Postpone if you are contagious according to the disease, have dyspnea or are clinically unstable. If symptoms appear during travel, notify the crew and follow safety procedures. After landing, seek evaluation when there are signs of severity. Planning, adequate vaccination and respect for privacy reduce risks without discrimination.
A **anemia** é uma redução da capacidade:
**Anemia** is a reduction in oxygen transport capacity, often related to low hemoglobin due to blood loss, iron deficiency, inflammation, kidney disease or bone marrow disorders. Weakness, paleness, tachycardia and shortness of breath reflect the effort to bring oxygen to the tissues. The number on the blood count needs to be read along with the speed of onset and the body's response: an acute loss does not behave like stable chronic anemia.

In the cabin, the **lower partial pressure of oxygen** adds to the reduction in the oxygen content of the blood. The CDC advises passengers to postpone travel with hemoglobin **below 8.5 g/dL**, except in stable chronic situations assessed individually; Acute uncontrolled bleeding requires delay. **Sickle cell disease** can be complicated by vaso-occlusive pain and lung problems, while the simple sickle cell trait does not have the same clinical significance.

**The passenger** needs control of the cause of the anemia, evaluation of symptoms and possible oxygen support. People with a recent sickle cell crisis should be evaluated before travel; the CDC considers it prudent to postpone travel when there has been a crisis in the **previous nine days**. **The crew member** follows its own requirements: in Brazil, RBAC 67, items 67.87 and 67.127, conditions hematological fitness for the assessment and determines unfitness in the face of hypercoagulability, bleeding disorder or coumarin oral anticoagulation.

Anyone flying with symptomatic anemia may experience **dyspnea, pre-syncope and functional disability**. Active bleeding can decompensate quickly; Venous thrombosis can embolize to the lung, producing chest pain and decreased oxygenation. The presence of very low platelets, spontaneous bleeding, or a recent thrombotic event changes the decision. Criteria for passengers, Brazilian pilots and pilots from other jurisdictions **should not be treated as interchangeable**.

**Anticoagulants** such as vitamin K antagonists, heparins and direct oral anticoagulants are prescribed to prevent or treat thrombosis in different indications. Undue suspension may precipitate a thromboembolic event; unattended use favors bleeding. For coumarin anticoagulation, the aforementioned Brazilian rule determines the candidate's ineligibility in the corresponding classes; Foreign guidelines may adopt different assessments. Do not extrapolate permissions from another country to the Brazilian CMA.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Treat the cause of anemia and confirm stability before traveling. Bring relevant exams, information about previous attacks, medical contact and prescription. Report any bleeding, chest pain, dyspnea, or asymmetric leg edema. On long trips, organize movement and individualized preventive measures; **do not adjust anticoagulants on your own**. The physician must document risk of bleeding, thrombosis, functional capacity and need for support.
A **vacinação** prepara a resposta imune:
**Vaccination** prepares the immune response against specific agents and reduces the likelihood of illness or complications. It is part of collective protection, but does not replace care with water, food, vectors, ventilation and hygiene. The schedule depends on age, vaccination history, destination, type of travel and clinical conditions. Routine vaccines, vaccines indicated by risk and immunizations required for entry into certain countries fulfill different roles and should not be confused.

The cabin environment does not make a vaccine ineffective by itself. What changes the response is mainly the immunological condition: **chemotherapy, immunosuppressants, transplantation and advanced HIV** can reduce protection or contraindicate live immunizations. A person without a spleen is at increased risk of infections caused by encapsulated bacteria because they have lost an essential part of their defense. Planning must also consider the risk at the destination, not just the flight, and may require specialized advice before immunizations. (See M1V5.)

**For the passenger**, it is recommended to update routine vaccinations and evaluate destination requirements in advance, especially when there is immunosuppression. The CDC suggests administering inactivated vaccines preferably before starting immunosuppression when possible; Live vaccines require precautions and may be contraindicated. **For the crew member**, vaccination must be integrated into the occupational health program; vaccine reaction, baseline condition and medication effects need to be compatible with operational safety.

Traveling without necessary protection can increase the risk of **preventable infection and transmission at destination**, particularly in vulnerable people. On the other hand, administering a live vaccine during severe immunosuppression may cause a major adverse event; Failing to check for contraindications is equally risky. Fever and post-vaccination malaise may temporarily reduce operational capacity, but do not automatically indicate transmissible infection. International certificates, when required, must comply with the health rules in force in the country of entry.

**Inactivated and recombinant vaccines** do not contain agents capable of replication and, in general, are preferred for immunosuppressed patients, although the response may be lower. **Live attenuated vaccines** require careful assessment of immune status. Immunosuppressive drugs can interfere with the response and safety of vaccination; treatments should not be interrupted just to receive a dose. Yellow fever vaccine, when relevant to the route, should be discussed with a specialist in the presence of contraindications, including possibilities for adjusting the itinerary.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Review your vaccination record before purchasing complex trips; Check destination recommendations, medical restrictions and required documents. Discuss with an infectious disease specialist, oncologist or assistant team when there is immunosuppression, HIV or hematological disease. Keep receipts without exposing clinical data beyond what is necessary. In case of major systemic reaction or decompensated condition, postpone air function or travel until evaluation. The objective is to protect the traveler without creating false guarantees.

O **HIV** compromete células do sistema:
**HIV** compromises immune system cells over time when left uncontrolled, but antiretroviral treatment allows many people to maintain an active life and stable health. HIV **is not transmitted by breathing cabin air, sharing seats or talking**. Risk of infection and clinical suitability should not be confused with stigma. The travel assessment considers viral suppression, immunological status, associated illnesses, medications and access to care on the itinerary.

A person with **well-controlled HIV**, undergoing treatment and follow-up, can generally travel as a passenger. The CDC warns that advanced immunosuppression and uncontrolled viral load increase the risk of opportunistic infections, especially in destinations with greater exposure. Cabin pressure does not in itself modify the virus transmission route. The presence of anemia, lung infection or other concomitant disease may reduce cabin oxygen tolerance and must be evaluated separately.

**For the passenger**, the decision must be individual and based on clinical stability, not just serology. Anyone with an active opportunistic infection or significant immunosuppression may need to postpone travel. **For the crew member**, it is essential to follow the applicable certification rules: the FAA requires a central assessment for HIV history, without an automatic decision by the examiner; In Brazil, the framework depends on clinical investigation and current fitness rules, with the protection of medical information.

Interrupting **antiretroviral therapy** may favor loss of virological control and risk of resistance. A trip without access to medication, with a poorly planned time zone or without care at the destination can make it difficult to continue. In those with advanced immunodeficiency, common infections can become more serious; fever and respiratory symptoms require attention. The presence of HIV alone does not mean an infectious risk for other passengers during everyday life.

**Antiretrovirals** must be maintained as prescribed, paying attention to interactions with antibiotics, prophylaxis, anti-malaria medications and other travel products. Inactivated vaccines are usually usable, while some live vaccines depend on the degree of immunosuppression and may be contraindicated. Carrying medications in identified packaging and appropriate documentation facilitates inspection without requiring unnecessary public exposure of the diagnosis. Legal entry restrictions vary between countries and should be checked before booking.

**How ​​to prevent and mitigate.** Organize the dose schedule to cross time zones without interruptions, take a reservation for delays and find medical care at the destination. Review vaccination and prophylaxis with an infectious disease specialist or travel medicine specialist. If there is an opportunistic disease, significant fever or decompensation, consider postponement. For the crew member, update documents and inform the examiner confidentially; the decision must be based on functional capacity and current aeromedical criteria.
O **sangue** leva oxigênio, distribui nu:
**Blood** carries oxygen, distributes nutrients, transports defense cells and participates in clotting. **RBCs**, through hemoglobin, carry a large part of the oxygen; leukocytes recognize infectious agents and platelets help contain bleeding. These mechanisms depend on the heart, lungs, bone marrow and the integrity of the vessels. Knowing this chain avoids confusing low oxygen pressure with a lack of hemoglobin.

In a pressurized commercial cabin, the partial pressure of oxygen is usually lower than at sea level, although the fraction of oxygen in the air remains practically the same. A healthy person compensates for this reduction. In **anemia**, there is less transport capacity; in sickle cell disease, reduced oxygenation can contribute to complications; in associated cardiopulmonary failure, the reserve decreases even further. Cabin pressure does not in itself cause cancer or HIV. (See M1V1 - II and M2V1.)

**For the passenger**, clinical stability, saturation, blood count and functional limitations guide the individual assessment; Being discharged or having a controlled diagnosis does not necessarily equate to being fit for a long trip. **For the crew member**, in addition to tolerating the cabin, it is necessary to maintain attention, resistance and operational safety. ANAC considers anemia, hematological diseases, coagulation and risk of incapacitation in the medical certificate rules, with distinction between classes.

An important hematological change can cause **intense fatigue, palpitations, dizziness, shortness of breath or fainting**. Bleeding, thrombosis or acute infection may appear or worsen away from care. Prolonged flight also favors venous stasis due to immobility, especially after surgery, in neoplastic activity and with previous thrombosis. This vulnerability arises from the state of coagulation and blood flow, not from the simple fact of being inside an airplane. (See M2V2.)

Useful tests include blood count, platelets and coagulation studies when indicated, always interpreted with symptoms, treatment and evolution. **Anticoagulants** reduce thrombotic events in specific situations, but require assessment of bleeding risk and interactions; they should never be interrupted just to travel. Chemotherapy, immunosuppression and some antivirals also require attention to adverse effects and continuity of the prescribed regimen.

**How ​​to prevent and alleviate it.** Plan the trip when the condition is stable; Bring a clinical report, list of medications and a reserve for delays. On long flights, move your legs and walk when it is safe to do so, respecting medical restrictions. Avoid boarding with bleeding, fainting, severe fever or uninvestigated dyspnea. The doctor must record the functional capacity, the possibility of assistance and, when necessary, the request for support from the airline.
