**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The hormonal diseases that weigh most on flying are **diabetes**, with the risk of **hypoglycaemia**, **thyroid** diseases, **obesity** and, more rarely, the cortisol deficiency of **Addison's disease**, which requires carrying cortisone at hand at all times. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, in mild changes under follow-up, to **non-invasive** treatment, which is the rule: diet, activity, oral medicines, **insulin** and replacement hormone. The **invasive** and ablative treatments are **thyroid surgery**, **radioactive iodine** and **bariatric surgery**, each with its grounding period. In the **pressurised** aeroplane, the cabin sits between 6,000 and 8,000 ft; in the **unpressurised** one, the greater climb enlarges the bubbles in the insulin pump, and above 10,000 ft hypoxia is easily confused with hypoglycaemia; in the single-pilot **helicopter**, the British insulin protocol, which requires a co-pilot, cannot be met.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Diabetes has no watchful-waiting option: **non-invasive** treatment starts with diet and activity, continues with oral or injectable medicines and reaches **insulin**, by pen, pump or with a continuous sensor. The **invasive** treatment is **bariatric surgery**, which can control type 2 diabetes in people with obesity (See M2V9 - V). The prognosis in flight is good with stable control: the passenger flies, and a crew member not on insulin returns after the waiting period for each new medicine. The grounding periods apply to every **change of medicine**, and a severe hypoglycaemia grounds until assessment. In the **pressurised** jet, long flights call for checking every 4 to 6 hours; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane and the **helicopter**, often single-pilot, there is no one to take the controls during a hypoglycaemia, and the British protocol, which requires a co-pilot, does not apply.
**Tratamentos e tipo de voo.** A insulin: **Treatments and type of flight.** Insulin is the most demanding **non-invasive** treatment for diabetes: pen, **pump** or continuous sensor change the travel routine but do not stop the passenger flying. For a crew member, the FAA requires **7 days** off flying at each change of pump or sensor. Management on the trip is **preventive**: a written plan for the time zone, spare insulin and frequent checks. In the **pressurised** jet, the cabin change already alters pump delivery; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, which climbs higher without pressurisation, the pressure change and the bubbles tend to be greater, and it is worth following the pump plan on every climb and descent; in the **helicopter**, repeated climbs and descents call for the same care, and the cold can affect the glucose meter and strips.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In **hypothyroidism**, treatment is **non-invasive**: levothyroxine every day, with control tests; the prognosis is excellent, and the return to flying comes with stable function. In **hyperthyroidism**, treatment starts **non-invasive**, with an antithyroid drug and a beta-blocker, and may move on to **radioactive iodine** or **thyroid surgery**, the **definitive** treatments. After them, a crew member stays grounded until recovery and stable function; a passenger follows the team's advice on distance and carries the proof because of airport alarms. With a stable thyroid, the type of aircraft does not change the rule; when uncontrolled, a racing heart has less margin in the hypoxia above 10,000 ft of the **unpressurised** aeroplane, and double vision weighs more in the low flying of the **helicopter**.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** A: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** Obesity has a basic **non-invasive** treatment, with diet, activity and, when indicated, a GLP-1-type medicine, respecting the crew waiting periods. The **invasive** treatment is **bariatric surgery**: in the United Kingdom, a crew member is **unfit for up to 3 months** after it, depending on the type of surgery and recovery, with reports confirming full recovery and no incapacitating side effects; **endoscopic** procedures shorten this period considerably. The passenger follows the advice for abdominal surgery, with about **10 days** before flying (See M2V10). Losing weight improves apnoea, blood pressure and blood sugar, and the prognosis in flight improves with them. In the **pressurised** jet, thrombosis on long flights weighs most; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, people with hypoventilation feel the hypoxia above 10,000 ft more; in the **helicopter**, space and weight on board also count in planning.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The diseases in this flight that weigh most on air travel are **anaemia**, **sickle cell disease**, clotting disorders and **thrombosis**, **cancer**, **communicable infections** and reduced immunity, as in uncontrolled **HIV**. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, in mild stable anaemia and sickle cell trait, to **non-invasive** treatment, which is most of it: iron, vitamins, anticoagulants, antibiotics, antiretrovirals and chemotherapy. **Invasive** treatments call for an interval before flying: **transfusion**, **surgery**, **biopsy**, drainage and catheter procedures. In the **pressurised** aeroplane, the cabin at up to 8,000 ft already reduces the oxygen supply for people with little haemoglobin; in the **unpressurised** one, above 10,000 ft without oxygen, that reserve goes faster, and the small cabin lacks the jet's filtration; in the **helicopter**, transport of someone bleeding or unstable is aeromedical, with a team and oxygen.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** N: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In mild stable anaemia and sickle cell trait, management is **watchful waiting**, with follow-up. **Non-invasive** treatment corrects the cause: **iron**, by mouth or into a vein, vitamin B12 or folic acid, control of bleeding and, in thrombosis, an **anticoagulant** for months or indefinitely. The **invasive** treatments are **blood transfusion**, **endoscopy** or **surgery** to stop bleeding and, in severe embolism, **thrombolysis** or a **catheter procedure**. The passenger's time limits: haemoglobin below **8.5 g/dL**, postpone; sickle cell crisis in the previous **9 days**, postpone; leg thrombosis, fly with stable anticoagulation; embolism, from **5 days** (IATA) or **2 weeks** (British society), with normal oxygen (See M2V2 - VII). In the **unpressurised** aeroplane, without oxygen above 10,000 ft, anaemia and sickle cell disease have less margin; in the **helicopter**, someone who is bleeding travels by aeromedical transport.

**Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In cancer, **watchful waiting** exists: **active surveillance** of some low-risk tumours and follow-up after treatment. The **non-invasive** treatments are **chemotherapy**, hormone therapy, **immunotherapy**, targeted therapies and **radiotherapy**. The **invasive** ones are **surgery**, **biopsy**, catheters and drainage of fluid from the chest or abdomen, and each has its interval: about **10 days** after abdominal surgery (See M2V10), **4 weeks** after removal of the drain from chest surgery and **1 week** after needle lung biopsy or bronchoscopy with biopsy (See M2V1), and **10 to 14 days** after skull surgery (See M2V6). Fever during chemotherapy, bleeding or very low platelets postpone any flight. The prognosis in flight depends on reserve, not on the diagnosis. After surgery, air left in the body expands more in the **unpressurised** aeroplane; in the **helicopter**, low flying expands it less, but the interval applies all the same.

**Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In mild viral illnesses, management is **watchful waiting**: rest, water and fever medicine, flying only without fever and without breathlessness. **Non-invasive** treatment is an **antibiotic** or **antiviral** when indicated. **Invasive** treatment is kept for severe forms: **hospital admission**, **drainage** of an abscess or of fluid around the lung. Some time limits are clear: in **measles**, isolation lasts until **4 days** after the rash begins, and the return depends on medical clearance; in drug-susceptible **tuberculosis**, flying only after **2 negative sputum smears**, which usually takes about **2 weeks** of adequate treatment; in **multidrug-resistant** tuberculosis, only after **2 consecutive negative cultures**; pneumonia with low oxygen postpones flying (See M2V1). In the **pressurised** jet, filters help but do not protect someone sitting near a sick person; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, the cabin is small and the occupants sit very close together.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In HIV there is no watchful-waiting option: **non-invasive** treatment with **antiretrovirals** is indicated for everyone and kept up without breaks, with prophylaxis when immunity is low. There is no invasive treatment for HIV; procedures come in only for complications. The prognosis is good: with a suppressed viral load, life and travel go on as normal, and the passenger flies without restriction. An active opportunistic infection or very low immunity calls for **postponing** until controlled. For a crew member, the decision belongs to the authority, based on stability and medicine side effects. Altitude and aircraft type do not change the virus: on the long-haul **pressurised** jet, the challenge is the **time zone** in dose timing; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane and the **helicopter**, the same medicine and symptom rules apply.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The digestive diseases that weigh most on flying are **reflux**, **gastritis** and **ulcer**; **diarrhoea**, **irritable bowel** and **inflammatory bowel disease**; **hepatitis**, fatty liver and **cirrhosis**; **gallstones** and **pancreatitis**; and **hernias** and abdominal operations. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, for symptom-free gallstones, mild irritable bowel and a hernia that does not hurt, to **non-invasive** treatment, which is most of it: diet, acid medicines, rehydration, bowel anti-inflammatories and hepatitis antivirals. The **invasive** treatments are **endoscopy**, **keyhole** or **open surgery**, gallbladder removal and, for a failing liver, **transplantation**. In the **pressurised** aeroplane, at 8,000 ft bowel gas grows by about **38%**; in the **unpressurised** one, at 10,000 ft, by about **50%**; in the **helicopter**, low flying expands it less, but, as in the light aeroplane, there is almost never a toilet.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** N: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In mild, occasional heartburn, management is **watchful waiting**, with habits. **Non-invasive** treatment is **acid medicine** and, when the **H. pylori** bacterium is present, antibiotics to eradicate it; in the United Kingdom, a crew member is **unfit during eradication** and returns on maintenance medicine. The **invasive** treatments are **endoscopy** to stop bleeding and **surgery** for perforation or stubborn reflux. The crew member's time limits: at the FAA, an ulcer active in the last **3 months** or that bled in the last **6 months** requires proof of **healing**; in the United Kingdom, unfit until recovery and demonstrated healing. A passenger with an ulcer that bled flies only when stable and with adequate haemoglobin (See M2V11 - II). In the **pressurised** jet, gas distends the stomach; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, it distends more; in the **helicopter** and the light aeroplane, a crisis far from a runway has no care.

**Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In mild travellers' diarrhoea and mild irritable bowel, management is **watchful waiting**: water, salts and diet. **Non-invasive** treatment is **oral rehydration**, loperamide when there is no fever or blood, antibiotics in selected cases and, in **inflammatory bowel disease**, bowel anti-inflammatories, immunosuppressants and **biologics**; **steroids** come in during a flare. **Invasive** treatment is **surgery**, such as removing part of the bowel, sometimes with a **stoma**. Crew time limits in the United Kingdom: inflammatory bowel disease only in stable **remission**, and for Class 1, **6 months** in remission on minimal medication, starting with a multi-crew limitation; after removing part of the colon for diverticulitis, at least **3 months**. Anyone with a stoma carries extra bags: gas also fills it on the climb. The **pressurised** jet has a toilet; the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter** almost never do, and a flare becomes an urgent landing.

**Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In isolated test abnormalities and early fatty liver, management is **watchful waiting**, with follow-up. **Non-invasive** treatment is losing weight, **stopping alcohol** and, in hepatitis B and C, **antivirals**, which cure hepatitis C in most cases. The **invasive** treatments are **banding of varices** by endoscopy, **needle drainage** of abdominal fluid, a catheter shunt inside the liver and **liver transplantation**. For a crew member, **oesophageal varices** mean unfit in the United Kingdom; after transplantation, fitness may return with a favourable gastroenterology assessment. A passenger with recent bleeding, new confusion or an abdomen very full of fluid postpones until stable. In the **pressurised** jet, the cabin already reduces oxygen for those with little reserve; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, above 10,000 ft, hypoxia can worsen the confusion of encephalopathy; in the **helicopter**, transport of someone bleeding is aeromedical.

**Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** For **symptom-free gallstones**, management is **watchful waiting**. **Non-invasive** treatment is that of the attack: pain relief, fluids, fasting in pancreatitis and antibiotics for gallbladder inflammation. **Invasive** treatment is **gallbladder removal**, almost always **by keyhole surgery**, and the **endoscopy** that removes a stone from the bile duct. The passenger's time limits: about **24 hours** after a simple laparoscopy and **10 days** after open abdominal surgery (UK CAA). The crew member's: at the FAA, gallstone pancreatitis, single episode, **1 month** after release, with the gallbladder removed and off pain medicine; alcohol-related or recurrent pancreatitis, **3 months** and an FAA decision; in the United Kingdom, symptomatic gallstones mean unfit until removed. The prognosis is good: once the gallbladder is removed, the colic does not return. In the **pressurised** jet, an attack on board calls for a diversion; in the single-pilot **helicopter** and **unpressurised** light aeroplane, sudden pain is incapacitation.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** For a painless **hernia**, management can be **watchful waiting**, and a crew member may be fit; a painful, trapped or femoral hernia means unfit until repaired. **Endoscopy** and **colonoscopy** are short **invasive** procedures: after colonoscopy, with a lot of gas in the bowel, the passenger waits **24 hours**. Simple **keyhole surgery** calls for about **24 hours**; **open** surgery, **10 days**. For a crew member in the United Kingdom, after hernia repair, unrestricted clearance comes only from **3 to 4 weeks**, with adequate recovery. The prognosis is good when the wound has closed, the bowel works and the pain is gone without sedating medicine. Gas left in the abdomen after surgery grows more in the **unpressurised** aeroplane; in the **pressurised** jet, the cabin at 8,000 ft is already enough to hurt; in the **helicopter**, low flying expands it less, but vibration and the effort of boarding weigh on a recent wound.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Each type of hypoxia has its diseases. **Hypoxic** hypoxia comes from **asthma**, **COPD**, **sleep apnoea**, **pneumothorax** and **pneumonia** (See M2V1 - VI to IX); **hypemic**, from **anaemia** and **carbon monoxide** poisoning (See M2V11 - II); **stagnant**, from **heart failure** (See M2V2). Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, in a small symptom-free pneumothorax followed with X-rays, to **non-invasive** treatment, which is most of it: **oxygen**, inhalers, **CPAP** and antibiotics. The **invasive** ones are the **chest drain**, lung **surgery** and, in severe carbon monoxide poisoning, the **hyperbaric chamber**. In the **pressurised** aeroplane, the cabin reaches 8,000 ft; in the **unpressurised** one, supplemental oxygen is mandatory above certain altitudes (See M1V2), and cabin heating from the exhaust can leak carbon monoxide; in the **helicopter**, which flies low, altitude hypoxia is rare, except in the mountains.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Asthma and COPD have no watchful-waiting option: **non-invasive** treatment is the basis, with maintenance and reliever **inhalers**, **stopping smoking**, **pulmonary rehabilitation**, vaccines and, in advanced COPD, **oxygen**. **Invasive** treatments are kept for severe emphysema: **lung volume reduction**, by surgery or by a **valve** placed during bronchoscopy, and **lung transplantation**; after chest surgery, a passenger waits **4 weeks** after removal of the drain (See M2V1 - VIII), and a crew member depends on the authority's decision. The prognosis in flight is good when the disease is stable. In the **pressurised** jet, those who need oxygen arrange the portable concentrator with the airline; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, above 10,000 ft without oxygen, saturation falls faster in COPD; in the **helicopter**, flight is low, but cold air and rotor dust can trigger an asthma attack.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In mild apnoea without sleepiness, management can start with habits: **losing weight**, sleeping on one's side and avoiding alcohol and sedatives at night. The standard **non-invasive** treatment is **CPAP**; for some, the **mouth appliance** that moves the jaw forward. **Invasive** treatments are kept for selected cases: **surgery** on the tonsils, palate or facial bones, the implanted **tongue nerve stimulator**, and **bariatric surgery** when there is obesity (See M2V9 - V). After any of them, a crew member only returns with **proven effective treatment**, usually by a new sleep study. The prognosis is good: once treated, sleepiness goes and fatigue risk falls. In the **pressurised** jet, the CPAP goes on board for night flights; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, flights are short and daytime, but sleepiness at the controls adds to hypoxia above 10,000 ft; in the single-pilot **helicopter**, there is no one to take over if sleep wins.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In a small, symptom-free pneumothorax, management can be **watchful waiting**: rest and **follow-up X-rays** until the air is absorbed, sometimes with **oxygen**, which speeds absorption. **Invasive** treatments come in when there is breathlessness or the pneumothorax is large: **needle aspiration**, a **chest drain** and, for recurrence or for those who fly for a living, **surgery**, by **video-assisted thoracoscopy** or thoracotomy, with **pleurodesis** to stick the lung to the chest wall. The time limits are above: 7 days after resolution for the passenger, months and the authority's decision for the crew member. The prognosis depends on surgery: without it, recurrence is the risk that weighs. Trapped air grows by about **38%** at 8,000 ft in the **pressurised** jet and about **50%** at 10,000 ft in the **unpressurised** aeroplane; in the **helicopter**, low flying expands it less, and aeromedical transport of someone with a pneumothorax usually calls for a **drain before take-off**.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Each law has its diseases. Boyle explains **barotrauma** of the ear, sinuses and teeth (See M2V3), **pneumothorax** (See M2V1 - VIII), the gas that distends the bowel after surgery (See M2V10) and the bubble in the eye after retinal surgery (See M2V4); Dalton explains **hypoxia** (See M2V1); Henry, **decompression sickness** (See M1V3 - II). Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, for a blocked ear that clears by itself in days, to **non-invasive** treatment, with decongestants, nasal steroids and **oxygen**, up to **invasive** treatment: opening the eardrum or placing a **ventilation tube**, **draining the chest** and treatment in the **hyperbaric chamber**. In each case, the time limit for flying is in the flight on that system. In the **pressurised** jet, trapped gas grows **1.4 times** at 8,000 ft; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, about **1.5 times** at 10,000 ft and **2.1 times** at 18,000 ft; in the **helicopter**, altitudes are lower, but climbs and descents repeat several times in the same flight.

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Dry air aggravates **dry eye**, **rhinitis** and the **dehydration** of those who already drink little, take a diuretic or have diarrhoea. Management is almost always **watchful waiting** and habit: water, less alcohol and caffeine. **Non-invasive** treatment is **artificial tears**, saline in the nose and, for contact lens wearers, switching to glasses on long flights. **Invasive** treatment, **intravenous fluids**, is kept for severe dehydration, which postpones flying until recovery. The prognosis is excellent: symptoms go within hours on the ground. In the **pressurised** jet, long cruise at 10% to 20% humidity dries most; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, flights are short, and what weighs is the heat of a cabin parked in the sun (See M1V4 - I).

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** A cabin at 8,000 ft is harmless for healthy people but weighs on those with little reserve: **COPD** and other lung diseases, **heart failure**, **anaemia**, **sickle cell disease** and **pulmonary hypertension** (See M2V1, M2V2 and M2V11). For them, management can be **watchful waiting** when resting saturation is above 95%; **non-invasive** treatment is **in-flight oxygen**, arranged with the airline beforehand through the **MEDIF**, after a **hypoxic challenge test** when indicated (See M2V1 - IX). There is no invasive treatment for cabin altitude; anyone who does not tolerate it even with oxygen **postpones** the trip until stable. In the **pressurised** jet, the cabin stays up to 8,000 ft; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, the cabin is the actual altitude, and the rule requires oxygen from 12,500 ft (See M1V2 - III); in the **helicopter**, almost never pressurised, low flying spares the body, except in the mountains.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** A: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** Decompression sickness **has no watchful-waiting option**: even if symptoms disappear on descent, the person is assessed. **Non-invasive** treatment starts in the aircraft, with **100% oxygen** and water, and the definitive treatment is **recompression in the hyperbaric chamber** (See M1V3 - IV), the most intensive treatment, with repeated sessions if symptoms remain. Treated early, the joint form usually heals without sequelae; the nervous system form can leave marks. The time limits: after a rapid decompression in flight, **24 hours** without flying; after chamber treatment, there is no consensus, and advice ranges from **72 hours**, the most cited, to **6 weeks**, with the hyperbaric doctor; a crew member returns only with clearance from the doctor and the authority. In the **pressurised** jet, the risk appears only in decompression; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, on every flight above 18,000 ft; in the **helicopter**, altitude risk is rare, but transport of a sick diver should be as low as possible.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Heat has three steps of illness, and each has its treatment. In **heat stress**, management is **watchful waiting** and habit: shade, a break and water. In **heat exhaustion**, treatment is **non-invasive**: lying down somewhere cool, removing excess clothing, cooling the skin and drinking water with salts. **Heat stroke** is an emergency: **rapid cooling**, preferably in cold water, and **invasive** treatment in hospital, with **intravenous fluids** and monitoring of the kidneys and brain. Anyone who has had heat stroke returns to flying only after recovery and medical assessment; exhaustion calls for at least a day's rest and full rehydration. In the **pressurised** jet, the risk is on the ground, with the cabin parked in the sun; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, the glazed cabin heats up like a greenhouse, the helmet and flight suit hold in heat, and low flying does not cool.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In **mild hypothermia**, treatment is **non-invasive**: shelter, dry clothing, insulation and **passive rewarming**, with a hot drink if the person is alert. In **moderate** hypothermia, **active rewarming** of the trunk comes in, with heat blankets and heat in the armpits and chest. In **severe** hypothermia, treatment is **invasive**, in hospital: warmed intravenous fluids and, in extreme cases, **extracorporeal circulation**, which warms the blood outside the body. **Frostbite** of fingers, nose and ears is treated by rewarming in warm water, and **surgery** on dead tissue comes only weeks later, when the limit of the injury becomes clear. The prognosis of hypothermia treated in time is good. In the **pressurised** jet, the risk is a forced landing in a cold region; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, heating is weak; in the rescue **helicopter**, the victim travels **lying down**, warmed and without abrupt movements, because of afterdrop.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The diseases linked to flight radiation are long-term ones: **cancer**, especially skin and breast cancer in studies of crew, and **cataract**. There is no treatment for the dose received; management is **watchful waiting** and surveillance: skin checks, **mammography** and eye examinations at the recommended ages. When disease appears, treatment is that of any case: **non-invasive**, such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy, or **invasive**, such as **cancer surgery** and **cataract surgery**, each with its time limit for returning to flying (See M2V11 - III and M2V4). In pregnancy, protection is **reporting early** and adjusting the roster. In the **pressurised** jet, high, long and polar routes receive the highest doses; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, which fly low, the cosmic dose is much lower, and what weighs is **ultraviolet** through the window.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In **temporary loss**, management is **watchful waiting**: quiet and protection, and hearing returns within hours. **Noise-induced loss** has no cure; treatment is **non-invasive**: stopping progression with protection and, when conversation becomes difficult, a **hearing aid**. **Sudden deafness**, in one ear, within hours, is urgent: treatment is **steroids** by mouth and, if that is not enough, an **injection into the ear**, an **invasive** treatment; the crew member does not fly until assessed (See M2V3). In profound loss, the **invasive** treatment is the **cochlear implant**. **Tinnitus** is treated with advice, background sound and therapy. The prognosis depends on protecting early: established loss does not come back. In the **pressurised** jet, the cabin is quieter; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, noise exceeds 90 dB, and a **protective headset** is essential.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Vibration is linked to **low back pain** and **neck pain**, and that of maintenance tools to **hand-arm vibration syndrome**, with white, numb fingers. In common low back pain, management is **watchful waiting** and movement: most improve within weeks. **Non-invasive** treatment is **physiotherapy**, exercise, non-sedating pain relief and adjusting the **seat** and posture. **Invasive** treatment, **spinal surgery**, is kept for a disc hernia pressing on a nerve that does not improve, and a crew member returns only after recovery and assessment (See M2V12). The prognosis is good when exposure is cut: seat, posture and breaks. In the **pressurised** jet, vibration is low; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the piston engine vibrates more; in the **helicopter**, the blades vibrate in exactly the band that blurs vision and tires the spine.

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** G weighs more on those with **low blood pressure**, **varicose veins**, **dehydration**, **anaemia** or medicines that lower blood pressure, and it injures the **neck** and **spine** of those who turn their head under load. After a G-LOC without injury, management is **watchful waiting**: the pilot recovers within seconds, but the episode is reported and reviewed. The fighter pilot's **neck pain** has **non-invasive** treatment, with **physiotherapy** and strengthening, and only rarely **invasive** treatment, with **surgery** for a disc hernia pressing on a nerve; return to high-G flying depends on recovery and the authority (See M2V12). Anyone who faints without G, on the ground, is investigated before returning (See M2V6 - III). In the **pressurised** transport jet, G barely exceeds 1.5; in the **unpressurised** aerobatic light aeroplane, the pilot almost never has an anti-G suit; in the **helicopter**, G is low, and what injures the spine is vibration and posture (See M1V6 - IV).

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Impact injuries are **spinal fracture**, **fractures** of the arms and legs, **head injury** and injuries to abdominal and chest organs. A **stable wedge fracture** is treated **non-invasively**, with relative rest, a brace and physiotherapy, and grounds the pilot from ejection-seat aircraft for **3 to 4 months** (See M1V8 - III). An **unstable** fracture or one threatening the spinal cord calls for **invasive** treatment: **surgery** with screws and rods. Head injury ranges from **watchful waiting**, in mild concussion, to **surgery** for a haematoma, with its own time limits (See M2V6). Return to flying depends on healing, strength and assessment (See M2V12). In the **pressurised** jet, protection is the **lap belt** over the pelvis and the brace position; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the **shoulder harness**; in the **helicopter**, impact is mainly **vertical**, and energy-absorbing seats protect the spine.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Some diseases make the inner ear even more deceptive: **positional vertigo**, **vestibular neuritis**, **Ménière's disease** and **vestibular migraine** (See M2V3 - III); **alcohol** also alters the inner ear and can keep acting on it after it has left the blood. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, because neuritis usually passes in weeks, to **non-invasive** treatment: a **repositioning manoeuvre** for positional vertigo, **vestibular rehabilitation**, medicine during attacks and migraine prevention. **Invasive** treatment is rare: an **injection into the ear** or **surgery** for Ménière's that does not respond. A crew member with vertigo does not fly and returns only without symptoms, after assessment. In the **pressurised** jet, two pilots and the autopilot give margin to someone who feels disoriented; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the long turn in cloud is the classic trap; in the **helicopter**, head movements and single-pilot flight favour **Coriolis**.

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Some eye diseases increase visual illusions: **cataract**, which scatters light and creates glare and halos at night; **vision in one eye only**, which removes part of depth perception; and **weak night vision** (See M2V4). Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, for an early cataract that does not yet interfere, to **non-invasive** treatment, with **glasses** of the right prescription and approach training, up to **invasive** treatment: **cataract surgery** and **refractive laser surgery**. In the United Kingdom, a pilot is unfit for at least **6 weeks** after cataract surgery, and refractive surgery requires more than **6 months** and, if requested, a glare test (See M2V4 - VII and VIII). With vision corrected, the prognosis is good. In the **pressurised** jet, instrument approaches and two pilots protect; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the visual night approach is where the **black hole** lives; in the **helicopter**, off-runway landings, in dust or snow, remove the references all at once.
**Tratamentos e volta ao voo.** A desori: **Treatments and return to flying.** Disorientation has no invasive treatment: what is treated is the **cause**. After an isolated, explained episode, management is **watchful waiting**: report, review the flight and train again. **Non-invasive** treatment is **training**: ground illusion demonstrations, simulator and instrument flying with an instructor; for those who get airsick or have a sensitive inner ear, **vestibular rehabilitation**. If the cause is a disease, its treatment comes in, sometimes **invasive**, such as cataract or Ménière's surgery (See M2V5 - II and III), and the return follows that disease's time limit. The prognosis is good: repeated training reduces episodes. In the **pressurised** jet, training is crew training, with task sharing; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the critical point is the pilot without an instrument rating who enters cloud; in the **helicopter**, training includes instrument recovery and landing without references.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Repeated hyperventilation usually has a cause: **anxiety**, **panic** and **fear of flying** (See M2V7 - II), but also **asthma**, pain and fever. In an isolated episode, management is **watchful waiting** and breathing: speaking slowly, counting breaths and, above all, checking the oxygen. **Non-invasive** treatment of the cause is **cognitive behavioural therapy**, breathing training and, when indicated, medicine, which has rules for crew (See M2V7 - II). There is no invasive treatment for hyperventilation. The prognosis is good: once anxiety is treated, attacks decrease. In the **pressurised** jet, the anxious passenger has a crew to help; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, above 10,000 ft, hypoxia and hyperventilation are confused, and oxygen comes first; in the **helicopter**, noise, vibration and low flying add stress.

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Those who most need the test and in-flight oxygen have **COPD**, **pulmonary fibrosis**, **pulmonary hypertension**, **cystic fibrosis** or heart disease with little reserve, or have just had **pneumonia**. Management is **watchful waiting** when resting saturation is above 95%; **non-invasive** treatment is **oxygen** in flight, with the flow set by the test, plus treatment of the disease: antibiotics for pneumonia, lung and circulation medicines. The most extreme **invasive** treatment is **lung transplantation**, and after it the return to flying is decided with the transplant team. The prognosis is good when oxygen is arranged beforehand. In the **pressurised** jet, the approved portable concentrator goes in the cabin; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, the cabin is the real altitude, and oxygen must be available already at lower altitudes; in the **helicopter**, transport of someone who depends on oxygen is aeromedical.

**O passageiro** autista é **PNAE** e te: **An autistic passenger** is a **PNAE** and has assistance and priority boarding. If they cannot understand the **safety instructions** or use the toilet without help, the airline requires a **companion**, provided free of charge or paid by the companion at up to **20%** of the fare. The lanyard is **optional** and does not replace a document when one is requested.
**O passageiro** com amputação é PNAE: t: **A passenger** with an amputation is a PNAE: they have assistance and priority boarding, and the crutch, wheelchair or spare prosthesis count as a **mobility aid**, free of charge. **Phantom pain**, felt in the limb that is no longer there, may worsen with travel fatigue; the medicine used for it often causes drowsiness. Walking in the aisle helps the residual limb and the leg veins (See M2V2 - VII).
**O passageiro** com visão monocular voa: **A passenger** with monocular vision flies without restriction. Watch out for the blind side in the aisle and at the airport and, if the other eye also sees poorly, take the same measures as someone with visual impairment: assistance, individual briefing and counting the rows to the exit.
**O passageiro** surdo ou com perda audi: **A passenger** who is deaf or hard of hearing tells the airline the **communication aids** they need and may ask for the **individual briefing** on emergency procedures. Telling the crew at boarding allows important announcements to arrive in writing or by gestures. **Hearing aids** and implants can be used on board.
**O tripulante** autista passa por avali: **An autistic crew member** undergoes an **individual** assessment. In the United Kingdom, autism **is not automatically disqualifying**: the examiner reviews psychology, neuropsychology or psychiatry reports and may request an updated assessment, and the candidate may start training with **progress reports**. The FAA does not list autism among the conditions in its psychiatric table: the decision is case by case. In Brazil, it falls under the RBAC 67 mental and behavioural assessment (See M2V7).
**O tripulante** com amputação passa por: **A crew member** with an amputation undergoes a **functional assessment** and, usually, a **medical flight test**. At the FAA, a stable amputation may receive a **SODA**. In the United Kingdom, people with a **below-knee** amputation usually fly with the prosthesis, preferably with a fixed ankle; **above the knee**, they often fly without the prosthesis, using their own technique on the pedals; with **both legs** amputated, they usually need an **approved hand control**. With an arm prosthesis, Class 1 requires a firm **thumb grip** on each hand.
**O tripulante** com paraplegia passa po: **A crew member** with paraplegia undergoes a **functional assessment** and a **medical flight test**. At the FAA, non-progressive paralysis is treated like an amputation and may receive a **SODA**. In an aeroplane, they usually need a **hand control** for the rudder and a **hand brake**; in the United Kingdom, these controls are approved only for **private flying**. In the **helicopter**, there is no approved hand control for the pedals, and the British authority has not yet certified a helicopter pilot with paraplegia.
**O tripulante** com transtorno psicosso: **A crew member** with a psychosocial disorder undergoes the mental and behavioural assessment, which is **individual** (See M2V7). What matters is function: attention, judgement, communication and stability under stress. A stable, treated diagnosis does not automatically mean unfitness, and the medicine used is also assessed. Intellectual disability that limits judgement and learning tends to prevent working as a pilot.
**O tripulante** precisa cumprir o teste: **A crew member** must pass the hearing test for the class. ANAC accepts someone who does not reach the thresholds if they pass speech discrimination and the whispered voice test, and at revalidation one ear may be enough. ICAO considers that a **hearing aid** is generally not accepted in flight for professionals. At the FAA, a deaf pilot may fly with the limitation **"not valid for flying where radio use is required"**.
**O tripulante** precisa de **adaptação*: **A crew member** needs **adaptation**: learning to use the depth cues of a single eye and to turn the head more to cover the field. ICAO accepts the exception after at least **6 months** of adaptation and a **flight test**; the FAA also asks for **6 months** and clears by special issuance in any class. ANAC accepts monocular vision at **revalidation** or at the initial exam after an accident or serious incident, with the other eye normal.
**Para o passageiro**, a regra é de **ac: **For the passenger**, the rule is about **access**. In Brazil, ANAC calls a **PNAE** (passenger needing special assistance) anyone with a disability, aged 60 or over, pregnant, breastfeeding, with an infant in arms or with reduced mobility or autonomy. Assistance runs from check-in to leaving the airport, **free of charge**, and boarding is **priority**.
**Para o tripulante**, a regra é de **se: **For the crew member**, the rule is about **operational safety**. ICAO allows a certificate to be issued to someone who does not meet a requirement when an **accredited medical conclusion** shows that safety is not at risk, taking into account skill, experience and operating conditions. When safety depends on a condition, it becomes a **limitation** written on the certificate.
A **amputação** pode ser de **membro inf: **Amputation** may affect a **lower limb**, below or above the knee, an **upper limb** or more than one limb. Many people use a **prosthesis**: mechanical, with an articulated knee or foot, or with electronic control and a battery. Others use crutches or a wheelchair. For flight, what counts is function with and without the prosthesis, the condition of the **residual limb** and pain.
A **cegueira** e a **baixa visão** mudam: **Blindness** and **low vision** change orientation at the airport, reading signs and notices, finding the seat and the way to the emergency exit. A blind person is a **PNAE**: they have assistance from check-in to leaving the airport, at connections and at disembarkation, and **priority boarding**, free of charge.
A **deficiência auditiva** vai da perda: **Hearing impairment** ranges from mild loss to **deafness**. In the cabin, announcements come through the **public address system** and the crew, and in an evacuation commands are spoken. For the pilot, hearing is the channel for the **radio**, audio alarms and conversation with the other pilot (See M2V3).
A **deficiência física** inclui parapleg: **Physical disability** includes paraplegia, tetraplegia, cerebral palsy, neuromuscular diseases and malformations, as well as amputations. For travel, the airline classifies the need: **WCHR** walks to the seat and climbs stairs but needs a wheelchair for distances; **WCHS** walks to the seat but cannot climb stairs; **WCHC** cannot move alone and must be carried to the seat; **STCR** travels on a stretcher.
A **deficiência intelectual** limita o r: **Intellectual disability** limits reasoning and autonomy; **psychosocial disability** results from long-term mental disorders, such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Other **hidden** disabilities include epilepsy, chronic pain, bowel diseases and mild hearing loss. The **sunflower lanyard** is Brazil's national symbol for these disabilities.
A **deficiência** pode ser **física**, *: **Disability** may be **physical**, **visual**, **hearing**, **intellectual** or **psychosocial**, and many are **hidden**: they are not visible at first sight. In flight, the question is never just the diagnosis. It is **function**: what the person can do alone, with help or with an adaptation, in a narrow, noisy environment that may demand a rapid evacuation.
A **visão monocular** é ter só um olho f: **Monocular vision** means having only one working eye, through loss, disease or severe low vision in the other. The visual field is smaller on the side of the missing eye and **3D vision at close range**, stereopsis, is lost. But **depth perception at a distance** remains: beyond a few metres, it comes from shadows, apparent size, perspective and motion (See M2V4).

Na **ANAC**, o candidato faz o exame com: At **ANAC**, the candidate is examined by the accredited examiner. If found unfit, they may appeal, and ANAC may, at its discretion, require a **flight proficiency test** and consult other examiners. Functional after-effects that may affect safety, monocular vision at the initial exam and hearing loss outside the tests are the most common points of discussion.
Na **Europa** e no **Reino Unido**, a de: In **Europe** and the **United Kingdom**, disability usually becomes a **limitation code**: only as or with a qualified co-pilot, only with a safety pilot and dual controls, no passengers, only with the approved prosthesis, only with approved hand controls, only with hearing aids or daytime only. The limitation goes with the certificate on every flight.
Na **FAA**, a condição **estática**, com: At the **FAA**, a **static** condition, such as amputation, non-progressive paralysis or deafness, may receive a **SODA** after a **medical flight test**. The SODA **does not expire**, but it is withdrawn if the condition worsens. Progressive conditions follow **special issuance**, with periodic reassessments.

Na cabine, a pressão mais baixa pode **m: In the cabin, the lower pressure can **change the volume of the residual limb**, and hours of sitting increase swelling: the prosthesis socket tightens or loosens. Carry adjustment socks or padding in your hand luggage. An electronic prosthesis should leave **charged**, with the charger and a spare battery in your hand luggage. Airport detectors and scanners may alter how electronic components behave: check the prosthesis after the security check.

Na prática, cada autoridade tem o seu ca: In practice, each authority has its own path. **ANAC** decides through the examiner and, on appeal, may require a **flight proficiency test**. The **FAA** uses the **SODA**, the statement of demonstrated ability, for stable conditions. **Europe** and the **United Kingdom** use limitation codes, such as "only with a co-pilot" or "only with the approved prosthesis".
No aeroporto, barulho, luzes, filas, toq: At the airport, noise, lights, queues, being touched at security, announcements and gate changes can cause **sensory overload**, with a meltdown, running away or shutdown. On the aircraft, add the tight space, engine noise, ear pressure and turbulence. Previewing each stage with photos or videos, rehearsing the route and bringing **noise-cancelling headphones** and comforting objects reduce unpredictability.

O **FREMEC**, cartão médico do passageir: The **FREMEC**, the frequent traveller's medical card, is for people with a **permanent, stable condition**, such as a visual, hearing or physical disability, who fly often. It is issued by the airline's medical service after a complete MEDIF or medical report and **waives a new MEDIF** on each trip as long as the condition and the assistance do not change. Validity is set by the airline, and any worsening must be reported promptly.
O **MEDIF**, formulário de informações m: The **MEDIF**, the medical information form, is the standard document an airline may request before accepting a passenger with an illness or disability. It has two parts: **Part 1**, completed by the **passenger**, with personal details, itinerary and assistance requested; and **Part 2**, completed by the **treating doctor**, with the diagnosis, associated conditions, oxygen, stretcher, companion, wheelchair, medicines, autonomy and the statement that the person can fly.
O **certificado médico aeronáutico** (CM: The **aviation medical certificate** (CMA, in Brazil) is not refused just because there is a disability. The starting point is the ICAO rule: someone who does not meet a requirement can be certified if the **accredited medical conclusion** shows that safety is not at risk, considering skill, experience and operation, with the necessary **limitations**.
O **cão-guia** viaja **sem custo**, na c: The **guide dog** travels **free of charge**, in the cabin, **on the floor next to the passenger**, with a harness and no muzzle. In Brazil, the pair carries the **ID card** with photo and the **tag** on the dog's neck, issued by the training centre or instructor, the up-to-date **vaccination card**, with multiple and rabies vaccines signed by a vet, and a collar, lead and harness with handle.
O **transtorno do espectro autista** (TE: **Autism spectrum disorder** (ASD) changes how a person perceives, communicates and handles change, with very different intensity from one person to another. In Brazil, an autistic person is **a person with a disability for all legal purposes** and may hold the **CIPTEA**, the identification card, valid for **5 years**. Autism is one of the **hidden disabilities**, and the **sunflower lanyard** can signal it.

**Tratamentos, reabilitação e tipo de vo: **Treatments, rehabilitation and type of flight.** After amputation, the path is **rehabilitation**: physiotherapy, gait training and **prosthesis** fitting, a **non-invasive** treatment that lasts months. **Phantom pain** ranges from **watchful waiting**, because it often lessens over time, to **non-invasive** treatment, with physiotherapy, mirror therapy and medicines, some prohibited for pilots; **invasive** treatment is **surgical revision of the stump** when there is localised pain, a wound or irregular bone. The passenger flies once the stump has healed, and a crew member returns after adaptation and the practical test. In the **pressurised** jet, hours of sitting swell the stump; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the cramped cabin makes putting on and taking off the prosthesis difficult; in the **helicopter**, the pedals require both legs.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Spinal cord injury and neuromuscular diseases have no treatment that restores lost function in most cases: the focus is **rehabilitation** and preventing complications. **Non-invasive** treatment includes physiotherapy, the right cushion, **spasticity** medicine and bladder and bowel care; intermittent bladder **catheterisation** is a simple procedure that travels along. The **invasive** treatments are **surgery** for a pressure injury, an implanted drug pump for spasticity and tendon and spinal operations, each with the surgeon's interval. An open **pressure injury** or a urinary infection with fever postpones flying. In the **pressurised** jet, the problem is the hard seat for hours; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, boarding requires a transfer by trained people.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Some causes of low vision are treatable: **cataract**, with surgery; **glaucoma**, with drops, laser or surgery; **diabetic retinopathy** and macular degeneration, with laser and eye injections (See M2V4 - VII and VIII). When the loss is permanent, treatment is **non-invasive**: **vision rehabilitation**, optical aids, screen readers, the cane and the **guide dog**. After eye surgery, the time limits of the eye flight apply; with **gas in the eye**, flying is prohibited until it is absorbed (See M2V4 - VIII). The prognosis depends on the cause: an operated cataract usually recovers vision; optic nerve loss does not. In the **pressurised** jet, orientation on board and assistance weigh more than altitude; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, the blind passenger needs a tactile safety briefing and someone to guide them out.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Monocular vision is rarely treated: management is **watchful waiting** and **adaptation**, and **non-invasive** treatment is protecting the good eye, correcting the prescription and training head scanning. When the cause is treatable, such as a cataract in the weak eye or a retinal detachment, **surgery** comes in, an **invasive** treatment with its own interval (See M2V4 - VIII). The prognosis is good after adaptation: many pilots fly with one eye. In the two-pilot **pressurised** jet, the other pilot covers the blind side; in the single-pilot **unpressurised** light aeroplane, lateral scanning weighs more, especially in traffic; in the **helicopter**, low flying near wires and obstacles requires turning the head all the time.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Hearing loss is treated according to its cause. **Wax** and otitis are resolved with simple measures; noise-induced and age-related loss are treated **non-invasively**, with a **hearing aid**; **sudden deafness** is urgent, with steroids and sometimes an injection into the ear (See M1V6 - II). The **invasive** treatments are middle ear surgery, the bone-anchored device and the **cochlear implant**, which can restore speech understanding to those with profound loss; after ear surgery, the passenger waits at least **10 days**, with ENT clearance (See M2V3 - III). Hearing aids and implants can stay on in flight. In the **pressurised** jet, written announcements help; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, loud noise masks speech, and a well-sealed headset is part of the treatment.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Autism is not a disease to be cured: treatment is **support**, almost all of it **non-invasive**. It includes **behavioural therapy**, speech therapy, occupational therapy and preparation for new situations, such as a **social story** of the trip and a visit to the airport. Medicine comes in only for associated conditions, such as anxiety, insomnia, ADHD or severe irritability, and sedating medicine changes the rule for crew. There is no invasive treatment for autism. The travel prognosis improves greatly with preparation and predictability. In the **pressurised** jet, the long flight, noise and full cabin are the challenge, and ear defenders help; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, noise and vibration are intense, and the flight should be explained beforehand, step by step.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In intellectual and psychosocial disability, treatment is **continuous** and almost all **non-invasive**: support, therapy, **medicines** on time and a crisis plan. **Watchful waiting** applies to those who have been stable for some time, changing nothing before the trip. **Invasive** treatment is rare: **hospital admission** and, in severe mood disorders, electroconvulsive therapy, with their own intervals and rules (See M2V7). In other hidden disabilities, such as epilepsy, kidney disease on dialysis and chronic pain, treatment follows the disease, and **dialysis** is scheduled around the flight. The travel prognosis depends on stability: a recent crisis postpones. In the **pressurised** jet, the crew can help in a crisis; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, there is no cabin crew, and the companion is even more important.

**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Ajuste o a: **How to prevent and ease it.** Adjust the seat before take-off, with the lower back supported and the arms reaching the controls without stretching. On long flights, stand up and stretch when it is safe. During a flare-up, prefer a simple painkiller and see a doctor if there is numbness or weakness. A crew member taking a medicine that causes drowsiness counts the waiting period before returning to the roster.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes do v: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before the flight, check that the injury is stable and that the cast has been on for the minimum time. During the flight, stand up and move your legs when it is safe, choose an aisle seat and rest your back against the seatback. Carry your daily medicine in your hand luggage and avoid sleeping on a sedating medicine during a long flight. Strong, enduring neck, trunk and leg muscles hold posture for longer, absorb vibration and share the load with the discs. **Return to flying** after an injury follows the same logic: those who return are those who have recovered function, not just those who no longer feel pain.

Voar com crise de dor tem dois riscos: a: Flying during a pain flare-up has two risks: pain that **draws attention away** and **limited movement**, which prevents turning the neck to look for traffic or reaching a control. **Weakness** in a leg can interfere with the pedal and with evacuation. For the crew member, hiding the condition from the examiner puts at risk the certificate and the investigation of any incident.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The diseases in this flight that weigh most in the air are **neck and back pain**, **disc hernia**, **fractures**, **osteoarthritis** and **arthritis**, **prostheses** and **amputation**. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, for common pain that improves within weeks with movement, to **non-invasive** treatment, which resolves most cases: **physiotherapy**, exercise, non-sedating pain relief, a **cast** or **splint**. The **invasive** treatments are **spinal surgery**, **fracture fixation** with plates and screws, **hip or knee replacement** and joint injection; the interval after them is set by the surgeon, and a crew member returns pain-free, without sedating medicine and with strength recovered. In the **pressurised** jet, hours of sitting and thrombosis weigh most; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the cramped cabin and the effort of boarding; in the **helicopter**, **vibration** and twisted posture, and in the fighter, the G load on the neck.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** N: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In neck or back pain without nerve signs, management is **watchful waiting** and active: keeping moving, which usually resolves it within weeks. **Non-invasive** treatment is **physiotherapy**, strengthening and common pain relief; a **muscle relaxant** or an **opioid** grounds for 5 half-lives (FAA). The **invasive** treatments are an **injection** near the nerve and **disc surgery**, for a hernia pressing on the nerve with weakness or pain that does not ease. At the FAA, disc surgery **does not disqualify**: the examiner clears a pilot who is **symptom-free, recovered, off medicine and without deficit**; a hernia with nerve symptoms goes to an FAA decision, and in Brazil means unfit (RBAC 67). The prognosis is good for most. In the **pressurised** jet, getting up and walking helps; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the fixed seat tires; in the **helicopter**, posture and vibration keep the pain going, and night vision goggles weigh on the neck.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** A: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** An undisplaced fracture may have **watchful-waiting** treatment, with protection and relative rest; most have **non-invasive** treatment, with a **cast**, **splint** or boot. **Invasive** treatment is **surgery**: reduction and fixation with **plates, screws or rods**, indicated when the bone is displaced, the joint is involved or the fracture is unstable. The passenger's time limits: **24 hours** after the cast for a flight under 2 hours and **48 hours** for a longer flight; after surgery, the interval is the surgeon's, and the risk of **thrombosis** weighs in the first weeks (See M2V2 - VII). A crew member returns when the bone has healed and strength and movement allow operating the controls and leaving the aircraft; for a spinal wedge fracture, **3 to 4 months** away from the ejection seat (See M1V8 - III). In the **pressurised** jet, a leg in a cast needs a seat with space; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the air splint expands more; in the **helicopter**, boarding and vibration hurt a recent fracture.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e certificaçã: **Treatments, prognosis and certification.** In mild **osteoarthritis** and **arthritis**, management is **watchful waiting** and exercise. **Non-invasive** treatment is physiotherapy, weight control, pain relief and anti-inflammatories and, in arthritis, disease-controlling medicines, some with rules for crew. The **invasive** treatments are joint **injection**, **arthroscopy** and hip, knee or shoulder **replacement**; in **amputation**, stump surgery and **prosthesis** fitting. After a joint replacement, the passenger follows the surgeon's interval and thrombosis prevention; a crew member returns pain-free and with function recovered. For amputation and stable limitation, the FAA can grant a **statement of demonstrated ability**, which does not expire, after a practical test. In the **pressurised** jet, request assistance 48 hours ahead; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, check reach to the pedals and controls; in the **helicopter**, the pedals and collective require both legs and both arms (See the special mission Disability and flying).
**Tratamentos e volta ao voo.** Depois d: **Treatments and return to flying.** After an injury, the return follows steps: relative rest, **rehabilitation** with physiotherapy, strength training and, finally, the practical test of operating the controls and leaving the aircraft. **Non-invasive** treatment is at the centre: **resistance exercise** for the neck and trunk, which also prevents the next attack. When there was **invasive** treatment, such as spinal surgery or a joint replacement, rehabilitation is longer, and a crew member returns only pain-free, without sedating medicine and with the examiner's clearance. The prognosis is good for those who keep training. In the **pressurised** jet, return requires enduring the duty period seated; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, strength for the controls and for a quick exit; in the **helicopter** and the fighter, neck endurance against the helmet, night vision goggles and G.

**Como prevenir e amenizar.** O ar conti: **How to prevent and ease it.** The air still holds 21% oxygen, but the pressure falls, and pressure decides how much oxygen reaches the blood. In a pressurised cabin, altitude usually stays at up to **8,000 ft**, which is enough for healthy people. Anyone with **lung or heart disease** should ask their doctor before the flight whether they need **in-flight oxygen** (See M2V1). In unpressurised aviation, the FAA rule requires **oxygen for the crew above 12,500 ft** for more than 30 minutes and always above 14,000 ft, because lack of oxygen removes judgement before giving any warning.

**Como prevenir e amenizar.** A atmosfer: **How to prevent and ease it.** The standard atmosphere is a ruler; the body responds to the day's air. At a **high airport on a hot day**, the pilot calculates **density altitude** before take-off, because the aircraft needs more runway and climbs worse. The altimeter must receive the **local pressure setting** whenever it is given, because a wrong setting changes the real height above the terrain. Anyone landing in a **high-altitude city** feels the low pressure on the ground: in the first days, **climb slowly**, drink water and avoid exertion and alcohol.

In jets, an **automatic controller** schedules the cabin's climb and descent according to the flight profile, and the crew monitors **cabin altitude**, **rate of change** and **differential pressure** on the panel.

For the crew, pressurisation is checked **before and during the flight**, and the cabin alert above 10,000 ft calls for **mask first and descent**, because the failure starts with no pain or warning.

**Como prevenir e amenizar.** A **hipóxi: **How to prevent and ease it.** **Hypoxic** hypoxia is prevented with pressurization and oxygen at the right altitudes. **Hypemic** hypoxia, by treating anemia before flying (See M2V11) and suspecting **carbon monoxide** in piston aircraft: headache, dizziness or drowsiness with the heater on call for oxygen and landing. O que muda no corpo da mulher na cabine,: What changes in a woman's body in the cabin, from menstruation to pregnancy and menopause?
Os **hormônios femininos**, sobretudo o: **Female hormones**, above all **oestrogen** and **progesterone**, do not control only the uterus and ovaries. They act on the **blood vessels**, **clotting**, **breathing**, the **bowel** and **fluid** retention. Over a lifetime, a woman goes through very different phases: the **menstrual cycle**, **pregnancy**, the **postpartum period** and **menopause**. Flying does not change the cycle by itself, but each phase changes how the body responds to the cabin.
**Menos oxigênio.** Com a cabine a até 8: **Less oxygen.** With the cabin at up to 8,000 ft, a healthy person's saturation falls to about 90% to 93% (See M2V1 - I). In **pregnancy**, progesterone stimulates breathing and oxygen consumption rises, but the fetus has its **own haemoglobin**, which holds oxygen more tightly. That is why, in a normal pregnancy, this drop does not usually harm the baby. It matters when reserve is already short: significant **anaemia**, **sickle cell disease**, **heart disease** and a fetus with **restricted growth**.
**Sangue que coagula mais.** O estrogêni: **Blood that clots more.** The oestrogen in the **combined pill** and in **oral hormone therapy**, **pregnancy** and the first weeks after **childbirth** increase clotting factors. Combined with hours of sitting, with the calf still, they favour **venous thrombosis** of the leg, which can travel to the lung (See M2V2 - VII). In pregnant women, the risk of thrombosis is at least **five times higher** than in non-pregnant women, although it remains low in absolute numbers.
**Gás, nariz e ar seco.** Na gravidez, a: **Gas, nose and dry air.** In pregnancy, progesterone slows the bowel, and trapped **gas** expands on the climb and bloats the abdomen (See M1V1 - II). **Pregnancy rhinitis** blocks the nose and makes it harder to clear the ear on descent (See M2V3 - II). The cabin's **dry air**, added to **nausea and vomiting** or **heavy menstruation**, dehydrates and lowers blood pressure; anyone who already has **anaemia** from bleeding feels hypoxia more (See M2V11 - II).
**Jornada, fuso e radiação.** O **fuso h: **Duty, time zones and radiation.** **Time zones** shift the timing of the **pill** and hormones, and a dose delayed beyond its limit no longer protects against pregnancy. The **sleep deprivation** of shift work has been associated with more **miscarriages**, besides weighing on performance (See M2V8 - V). And the **fetus** is more sensitive to **cosmic radiation** than the adult: once the pregnancy is reported, it is recommended that it receive at most **1 mSv** until the end of pregnancy (See M1V5 - III).
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The conditions in this flight are **pregnancy** and its complications, **childbirth**, **pregnancy loss** and **ectopic pregnancy**, **period pain** and **heavy bleeding**, **endometriosis**, **hormonal contraception** and **menopause**. Management ranges from **watchful waiting**, in a normal cycle and an uncomplicated pregnancy, to **non-invasive** care, with medicines, hormones and compression stockings, and **invasive** care: caesarean section, curettage and gynaecological surgery, each with its own timeline. In a **pressurised** jet, the hours of sitting and the cabin at 8,000 ft weigh most; in an **unpressurised** light aircraft, the real altitude and the lack of a toilet; in a **helicopter**, vibration and the belts over the abdomen.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes do v: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before the flight, check which phase you are in and what it requires: the week of pregnancy on the outbound and return dates, the pill time in the destination time zone, haemoglobin if bleeding is heavy. During a long flight, **drink water**, get up and move your calves, choose an **aisle** seat and wear the **belt low**, over the hips. A crew member reports pregnancy and any new hormonal medicine to the examiner, because both change the decision on the certificate.

Até quando a gestante pode voar como pas: Until when can a pregnant woman fly as a passenger, and why does a pregnant crew member stop earlier?
A **gestação** dura cerca de 40 semanas,: **Pregnancy** lasts about 40 weeks, divided into three **trimesters**. The body adapts in every system: **blood volume** increases, the **heart** beats faster, **breathing** deepens, blood becomes more prone to **clotting** and, early on, **nausea** and sleepiness are common. In the cabin, a normal pregnancy tolerates the small fall in oxygen well, because the fetus has its own haemoglobin (See M2V13 - I). What changes the risk is not altitude, but the **distance from a hospital** if something goes wrong.
As complicações obstétricas são mais fre: Obstetric complications are more frequent in the **first** and **third trimesters**. Early on, **bleeding**, threatened **miscarriage** and **ectopic pregnancy** weigh most; late on, **preterm labour**, **pre-eclampsia** and **placental** problems. On board, none of these can be treated, and the aircraft may need to **divert**. Added to this are **thrombosis** from hours of sitting, **nausea**, an abdomen bloated by gas and an ear that will not clear because of a blocked nose (See M2V3 - II). **Multiple** pregnancies, a low-lying placenta and a fetus with restricted growth carry more risk.
**Para a passageira**, a maioria das com: **For the passenger**, most airlines accept flights up to **36 weeks** in a single pregnancy and up to **32 weeks** in a multiple one; after **28 weeks**, many ask for a **certificate** with the expected date of delivery and confirmation that the pregnancy is progressing without complications. The gestational age **on the return date** counts, not just on the outbound flight. Pregnant women in **labour**, with **bleeding**, placental abruption, current or previous **pre-eclampsia**, or other complications that the obstetrician contraindicates should not fly.
**Para a tripulante**, a regra muda de p: **For crew**, the rule changes from country to country. In **Brazil**, RBAC 67 finds a 1st or 2nd class applicant **unfit** as soon as pregnancy is confirmed: she must inform the examiner or ANAC, and the certificate is suspended until reassessment after the birth. The exception is the 4th class, in which a low-risk, monitored pregnancy may be found fit **between the 12th and 26th week**. **ICAO** recommends the same interval, with obstetric assessment. Under **EASA**, a pilot may fly until the end of the **26th week**, in Class 1 only with another pilot on board. For the **FAA**, a normal pregnancy is **not disqualifying**, and the examiner advises on the third trimester and the seat belt.
Voar sem condição cobra do corpo e da ca: Flying when unfit takes its toll on the body and the career. **Bleeding**, **pre-eclampsia** or **preterm labour** on board endanger mother and baby, far from an obstetric centre, and may force a **diversion**. A passenger beyond the limit may be **refused boarding**, and **travel insurance** may not cover the birth or the newborn. In Brazil, a crew member who flies pregnant without informing the examiner breaches RBAC 67, and the flight takes place without a valid certificate, with consequences for insurance and any investigation.
Os remédios pedem cuidado dobrado. Para: Medicines need double care. For pain and fever, **paracetamol** is the choice; **anti-inflammatories**, such as ibuprofen, should be avoided from the **20th week**, because they can reduce the fluid around the baby. **Nausea** has medicines that are safe in pregnancy, but some cause **sleepiness**. Women at high risk of thrombosis may be given **heparin** by the obstetrician before a long flight; for the rest, movement, water and **compression stockings** are enough. **Iron** stays on its usual schedule.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The complications that weigh most are **pre-eclampsia**, **gestational diabetes**, **placenta praevia**, **anaemia** and **threatened preterm labour**. An uncomplicated pregnancy calls for **watchful** management: up-to-date antenatal care and the airline's rules. **Non-invasive** treatment includes blood pressure medicine, insulin or diet for diabetes, iron and rest; **invasive** treatment includes cervical cerclage and **caesarean section**, which end flying until the obstetrician clears it. In a **pressurised** jet, the risk is the distance from hospital; in an **unpressurised** light aircraft, the real altitude and turbulence; in a **helicopter**, vibration and the belts over the abdomen.
**Não voe hoje** com sangramento, contra: **Do not fly today** with bleeding, contractions or abdominal pain, leaking fluid, a severe headache with blurred vision or sudden swelling, fever, or pain and swelling in one leg. Before the ticket is bought, the obstetrician checks the **gestational age on the outbound and return dates**, whether the pregnancy is single or multiple, the placenta, blood pressure, haemoglobin and any history of preterm birth, and issues the certificate the airline requires.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Escolha o: **How to prevent and ease it.** Choose an **aisle seat** near the toilet and wear the **belt below the bump**, over the hips; if there is a shoulder strap, it goes between the breasts. **Walk** every one or two hours, move your calves while seated, drink water and wear **compression stockings** on a long flight. Carry the antenatal card, the certificate and your medicines in hand luggage. Avoid fizzy drinks and gas-forming foods before the flight, and swallow or yawn on descent to clear your ears.

Quando voltar a voar depois do parto ou: When can you fly again after childbirth or a loss, and what changes when breastfeeding?
Depois do parto, o corpo leva cerca de *: After childbirth, the body takes about **six weeks** to return to its previous state: this is the **puerperium**. The uterus shrinks, postpartum bleeding decreases gradually, and blood remains **more prone to clotting** in the first weeks. Many mothers reach this phase with **anaemia** and little sleep. A **caesarean section** adds abdominal surgery. **Pregnancy loss**, spontaneous or not, and **ectopic pregnancy**, which implants outside the uterus, also leave bleeding, pain and fatigue, besides the emotional burden.
Flying worsens what has not yet healed. In the weeks after childbirth, **thrombosis** is more likely than at any stage of pregnancy, especially after a caesarean section, and hours of sitting add to the risk (See M2V2 - VII). **Anaemia** weighs more in the cabin (See M2V11 - II), and gas trapped in the operated abdomen expands on the climb (See M1V1 - II). When **ectopic pregnancy** is suspected, a rupture causes **internal bleeding** that kills without prompt surgery, so any pain or bleeding in early pregnancy rules out flying until a diagnosis is made.
**Para a passageira**, não há um prazo ú: **For the passenger**, there is no single timeline after childbirth: after an uncomplicated vaginal birth, the obstetrician decides, based on bleeding, blood pressure and haemoglobin; after a **caesarean section**, the timeline follows that of abdominal surgery (See M2V10). After a **miscarriage**, threatened or complete, the IATA medical manual accepts flying once the woman is **stable, with no bleeding and no pain for at least 24 hours**. **For crew**, in Brazil, RBAC 67 requires a **new revalidation exam** after maternity leave or the end of pregnancy, and return is at the discretion of the examiner or ANAC. Under EASA, return comes **after recovery**; the UK CAA grounds crew after a pregnancy loss or termination until a report confirms full recovery and, for Class 1, also requires a psychological assessment.
Voltar cedo demais tem custo. A bordo, u: Returning too early has a cost. On board, **haemorrhage**, **pulmonary embolism** or a wound infection cannot be treated, and the aircraft may need to divert. A crew member who resumes duty **without the postpartum reassessment** flies without a valid certificate in Brazil, with consequences for insurance and any investigation. And postpartum fatigue, added to the sleep deprivation of a newborn, lowers attention like any fatigue (See M2V8 - V).
Na **amamentação**, os analgésicos comun: When **breastfeeding**, common painkillers such as **paracetamol** and **ibuprofen** are compatible. **Heparin** prescribed after childbirth to prevent thrombosis increases bleeding in trauma, and a crew member using it is assessed by the examiner (See M2V11 - II). **Postpartum depression** is common and treatable; intense sadness or thoughts of harming oneself or the baby call for immediate medical help, and a crew member's antidepressant follows its own rules (See M2V7 - II). For a travelling mother, **breastfeeding or offering a bottle during climb and descent** helps the baby clear its ears.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The conditions that weigh most are **postpartum haemorrhage**, **anaemia**, **thrombosis**, **infection** of the wound or uterus, **postpartum depression**, **miscarriage** and **ectopic pregnancy**. Management is **watchful** in an uncomplicated puerperium and in a complete miscarriage without bleeding; **non-invasive** treatment includes iron, antibiotics, medicine to complete emptying of the uterus and heparin; **invasive** treatment includes **curettage**, surgery for ectopic pregnancy and caesarean section. In a **pressurised** jet, hours of sitting weigh most; in an **unpressurised** light aircraft and a **helicopter**, the lack of a toilet and vibration over the operated abdomen.
**Não voe hoje** com sangramento que enc: **Do not fly today** with bleeding that soaks a pad within an hour, fever, severe abdominal pain, pain or swelling in one leg, breathlessness or chest pain; nor with pain or bleeding in early pregnancy without a diagnosis. The doctor checks the type and date of birth, **haemoglobin**, blood pressure, healing and mood; for a crew member, they record full recovery for the revalidation exam.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Nas primei: **How to prevent and ease it.** In the first weeks after childbirth, choose **short flights**, an **aisle seat** and leg movement, with water and compression stockings if the doctor recommends them. Carry pads, your medicine prescriptions and, if breastfeeding, a breast pump in hand luggage; **breast milk** is usually exempt from liquid rules, but check with the airport. Offer the breast or bottle to the baby during climb and descent. A crew member books the revalidation exam before going back on the roster.
