Cólica, sangramento intenso, pílula e fu: Period pain, heavy bleeding, the pill and time zones: what changes the decision to fly?
O **ciclo menstrual** dura, em geral, de: The **menstrual cycle** usually lasts from 21 to 35 days. Oestrogen prepares the uterus, ovulation occurs mid-cycle and, without pregnancy, the fall in progesterone triggers **menstruation**, lasting three to seven days. **Period pain**, **dysmenorrhoea**, comes from substances that contract the uterus. **Heavy bleeding** causes iron loss every month and leads to **anaemia** (See M2V11 - II). In **endometriosis**, tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside it and causes pain that can be severe. **Hormonal contraceptives** use oestrogen and progestogen, or progestogen alone, to prevent ovulation.
No voo, o ciclo pesa de três jeitos. A *: In flight, the cycle weighs in three ways. **Severe period pain** and the pain of endometriosis distract and, in intense cases, incapacitate. **Heavy bleeding** with anaemia adds dizziness and fatigue to the cabin at 8,000 ft, and light aircraft and helicopters almost never have a toilet. And the **oestrogen in the combined pill** increases clotting: after flights of **more than 4 hours**, the risk of thrombosis already doubles, and the hormone adds to it (See M2V2 - VII). Finally, **time zones** shift the pill time, and a dose delayed beyond the limit no longer protects.
**Para a passageira**, nada disso impede: **For the passenger**, none of this prevents flying: with the combined pill and a long flight, anti-thrombosis measures apply; with heavy bleeding and anaemia, the doctor checks haemoglobin beforehand. **For crew**, the FAA states that **contraceptives and hormone therapy are not disqualifying** if there are no side effects, and the UK CAA accepts them without distracting effects. The UK CAA grounds anyone under **specialist investigation for heavy bleeding** until the report and a normal haemoglobin, and anyone with a **first diagnosis of endometriosis**, until symptom-free on minimal pain relief. After **gynaecological surgery**, minimum periods range from **1 week** after curettage to **12 weeks** after open hysterectomy. In Brazil, the examiner assesses.
Voar sem condição tem custo. Uma **cólic: Flying when unfit has a cost. **Incapacitating period pain** on approach or **fainting** from anaemia takes a crew member out of duty in the most critical phase. A **thrombosis** that nobody prevented can become a **pulmonary embolism** hours after landing. And a new medicine or condition not declared to the examiner leaves the certificate irregular, with consequences for insurance and any investigation.
Os **anti-inflamatórios**, como ibuprofe: **Anti-inflammatories**, such as ibuprofen and naproxen, treat period pain without causing sleepiness. The **pill** and the hormonal or copper **IUD** do not prevent flying. When changing time zones, what matters is the **interval** between doses: with the combined pill, a dose counts as missed when it is more than **24 hours** late; with the traditional progestogen-only pill, the window is **3 hours**, and with desogestrel, **12 hours**. That is why you keep home time or shift gradually. Medicines to **delay menstruation** or for **heavy bleeding** are checked with the examiner before flying.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The conditions that weigh most are **dysmenorrhoea**, **heavy uterine bleeding**, **fibroids**, **polycystic ovary syndrome** and **endometriosis**. Management is **watchful** for mild period pain; **non-invasive** treatment includes anti-inflammatories, the pill or a hormonal IUD, iron and, in polycystic ovary syndrome, hormones or metformin; **invasive** treatment includes **laparoscopy**, fibroid removal and **hysterectomy**, each with its own time off flying. In a **pressurised** jet, thrombosis on a long flight and time zones weigh most; in an **unpressurised** light aircraft and a **helicopter**, the lack of a toilet.
**Não voe hoje** com sangramento que enc: **Do not fly today** with bleeding that soaks a pad within an hour, dizziness or fainting, sudden severe pelvic pain or, for pill users, pain and swelling in one leg, breathlessness or chest pain. The doctor checks **haemoglobin**, the type of contraceptive and thrombosis risk factors; for a crew member, they record the diagnosis, the treatment and any side effects.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Leve na ba: **How to prevent and ease it.** Carry pads or a menstrual cup, the anti-inflammatory you already use and your pill pack in hand luggage. On a long flight, if you take the combined pill, **walk**, move your calves, drink water and wear **compression stockings** if you have another risk factor. Set an alarm to take the pill on **home time**. Before flying in an aircraft with no toilet, use protection for the expected flow. A crew member tells the examiner about their contraceptive and any new medicine.

A **menopausa** é a última menstruação,: **Menopause** is the last menstrual period, confirmed after **12 months** without menstruating; it usually arrives between **45 and 55**. Before it comes **perimenopause**, years of irregular cycles. As oestrogen falls, **hot flushes**, **night sweats**, **poor sleep**, **mood** changes, difficulty **concentrating** and vaginal dryness appear. Inside, bone loses mass faster and the risk of **heart disease** rises. Surgical removal of the ovaries causes a **surgical menopause**, with sudden onset.
No voo, os sintomas somam-se ao ambiente: In flight, the symptoms add to the environment. A **hot flush** in a warm cockpit, with a headset and uniform, is uncomfortable and distracting. **Poor sleep** adds to night duties and time zones, and fatigue lowers attention (See M2V8 - V). **Oral hormone therapy** increases the risk of thrombosis, which a long flight multiplies (See M2V2 - VII); through the skin, as a patch or gel, this increase does not appear. In **Brazil**, RBAC 67 lists as a cause of unfitness changes that, in the judgement of the examiner or ANAC, result from **replacement hormones**: the decision is individual.
Flying without adjusting treatment has a cost. **Fatigue** built up from poor sleep increases errors, and a new sedating medicine taken without telling the examiner leaves the certificate irregular, with consequences for insurance and any investigation. An unprevented **thrombosis** can become an embolism hours after landing.
A **terapia hormonal** é o tratamento ma: **Hormone therapy** is the most effective treatment for hot flushes; women with a uterus receive oestrogen with progestogen. The **transdermal** route is the one that least affects clotting. **Non-hormonal** options, such as some **antidepressants**, **gabapentin** and newer medicines, help those who cannot use hormones, but several cause **sleepiness**, and a crew member's antidepressant follows its own rules (See M2V7 - II). **Calcium**, **vitamin D** and weight-bearing exercise protect bone. Any new medicine is checked with the examiner before flying.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The conditions that weigh most are **vasomotor symptoms**, **insomnia**, **osteoporosis**, **heart disease**, which becomes more frequent after menopause, and **postmenopausal bleeding**, which always needs investigation. In a **pressurised** jet, thrombosis and time zones weigh most; in an **unpressurised** light aircraft and a **helicopter**, the heat of a cabin parked in the sun (See M1V4 - I).
**Não assuma a função** com sono tão rui: **Do not take up duty** with sleep so poor that it causes daytime sleepiness, in the first weeks of a new sedating medicine or with hot flushes that interfere with the task. Bleeding after menopause does not prevent flying by itself, but it needs investigation. The doctor checks symptoms, sleep, the route and dose of the hormone, thrombosis and heart disease risk factors, and bone density.

O que o ar seco, as horas sentado e o fu: What do dry air, hours of sitting and time zones do to the kidneys and bladder?
Os **rins** filtram o sangue o dia intei: The **kidneys** filter the blood all day long: about **180 litres** of filtrate pass through them each day, and almost all of it returns to the blood. What is left becomes **urine**, which flows down the **ureters** to the **bladder** and leaves through the **urethra**. Along the way, the kidney balances the body's water, salt and acidity and produces **erythropoietin**, the hormone that tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells. In flight, the kidney works the same way; what changes is the water coming in, the time spent sitting and the timing of medicines.
O **ar seco** da cabine tira água pela r: The **dry air** of the cabin removes water through breathing and the skin without you noticing (See M1V1 - IV). **Thirst** only appears once about **1.5 litres** have been lost, roughly **2% of body weight**. Many passengers and crew also drink less to avoid going to the toilet, and pilots avoid leaving the flight deck on long flights. The kidney responds by holding on to water: urine becomes **dark and concentrated**, the setting in which crystals clump together and form **stones** (See M2V14 - II).
A cabine a até **8.000 ft** tem menos ox: The cabin at up to **8,000 ft** has less oxygen (See M1V1 - I). A healthy kidney notices no difference, but people with **chronic kidney disease** often have **anaemia**, because erythropoietin is lacking: with less haemoglobin to carry the oxygen that remains, tiredness, breathlessness and dizziness appear sooner (See M2V11 - II and M2V14 - III). **Gas expansion** matters after keyhole surgery, when gas left in the abdomen grows during the climb (See M1V1 - II and M2V14 - V).
As **horas sentado** também mexem com a: The **hours of sitting** also affect the bladder. The seat-belt sign, the toilet queue and sleep make people **hold their urine** for longer. In a man with an **enlarged prostate**, an over-full bladder, **alcohol** and drowsy-making medicines, such as some **antihistamines** and travel-sickness remedies, can block the outflow of urine: this is **urinary retention**, which is painful and needs a catheter (See M2V14 - IV). Alcohol and caffeine also make you pass more urine and add to water loss.
O **fuso horário** mexe com os remédios: The **time zone** affects kidney medicines. **Diuretics**, blood-pressure tablets and a transplant recipient's **immunosuppressants** all have set times. Many transplant teams accept **2 to 3 hours of leeway** in timing and, on trips of **up to 3 time zones**, the medicine can stay on home time; beyond that, the change-over plan is agreed with the team (See M2V8 - IV). A diuretic taken before a long flight makes you pass urine just when the toilet is hard to reach.
Quem sente primeiro é quem já tem o rim: Those who feel it first are people whose kidney or bladder is already at its limit: anyone who has had **kidney stones**, has **chronic kidney disease**, is on **dialysis** or has received a **transplant**, a man with an **enlarged prostate**, anyone with a **catheter** or a **urinary infection**, and anyone who has just had **urological surgery**. For crew members, the biggest problem is **renal colic**, which starts without warning and can take someone out of the controls within minutes (See M2V14 - II).
Aviation knows kidney stones well. In a study of **US Army aviators**, the annual incidence was **4.7 cases per 1,000** aviators, about **double** the reference male population, and the flying environment, with dehydration, was considered a suspect. On board, colic, the fever of an infection or a bladder that will not empty can lead to a **diversion**; for crew members, the authority's rules, the medical certificate and insurance also weigh in (See M2V14 - II to V).
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes do v: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before the flight, arrive well hydrated and go to the **toilet** before boarding. During the flight, drink **water before you feel thirsty**, in sips spread out over time, and use the colour of your urine as a guide: **pale** is a good sign. Go easy on **alcohol** and **caffeine**, choose an **aisle seat** if you pass urine often and get up when the seat-belt sign allows. Carry your medicines in **hand luggage**, with extra, and adjust the timing to the time zone with your doctor. Crew members keep a **bottle in sight** that lets them measure what they have drunk, and do not put off the toilet until after landing.

Por que a pedra nos rins tira o piloto d: Why does a kidney stone ground a pilot, and when can pilots and passengers fly again?
A **pedra nos rins**, ou **cálculo renal: A **kidney stone**, or **renal calculus**, forms when urine becomes concentrated and crystals of **calcium**, **uric acid** and other salts clump together. While the stone sits in the kidney, it is usually quiet. When it breaks loose and travels down the **ureter**, a narrow tube, it gets stuck and blocks the urine: the kidney swells behind the blockage and **renal colic** follows, one of the worst pains there is, in the back or side and moving down to the groin, with **nausea**, **sweating** and sometimes **shock**.
O voo não cria a pedra sozinho, mas ajud: Flying does not create the stone on its own, but it helps: **dry air** and too little water concentrate the urine (See M2V14 - I). What makes a stone dangerous in aviation is something else: **no one can predict** when it will move or how badly it will hurt. Smooth stones **smaller than 5 mm** often pass by themselves, yet they can still cause pain, nausea, sweating or shock severe enough to **incapacitate** a pilot. On board, far from an intravenous painkiller, a passenger's colic often ends in a **diversion**.
O tratamento segue três caminhos. O **ex: Treatment follows three paths. **Expectant** management suits a small stone: painkillers, water and waiting, straining the urine to catch the stone. **Non-invasive** treatment includes medicine that relaxes the ureter and **extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy** (ESWL), which breaks the stone with shock waves from outside the body; fragments keep moving down for **up to about 2 weeks**. **Invasive** treatment includes **ureteroscopy** with a laser, often with a **double-J stent** left in the ureter for a few weeks, and surgery through the skin for large stones. The outlook is good, but stones **come back** in many people, which is why prevention matters so much.
**Quando pode voar.** O **passageiro** e: **When you can fly.** A **passenger** with colic, fever or vomiting does not fly. After **ESWL**, the advice is not to travel abroad for the following **2 weeks**, because a fragment can get stuck far from home; a little blood in the urine for **1 to 2 days** is expected. With a **double-J stent**, travel is safe if your health allows, but the stent bothers many people and there is a small chance of needing medical help. For **crew members**, the FAA clears anyone whose last episode was **5 or more years ago**, without symptoms, and anyone who passed **a single stone** less than 5 years ago with imaging showing no retained stone; retained stones without symptoms follow the **CACI**; complications, symptoms or a cause of recurrence go to an **FAA decision**.
Na **ANAC**, a sequela de doença dos rin: Under **ANAC** rules, after-effects of kidney disease with obstruction, including from **urolithiasis**, make the applicant **unfit**, unless medically investigated and judged not to affect flight safety. In Europe, a pilot with a urinary stone is **unfit** until investigated; while awaiting treatment, they may fly **only with another pilot on board** (OML, in Class 1); after successful treatment, they return without restriction; with a **residual stone in the kidney**, Class 1 keeps the OML. In New Zealand, a residual stone after repeated colic is usually seen as an **unacceptable risk**.
**Voar sem liberação** cobra caro. No co: **Flying without clearance** has a high price. At the controls, colic is **sudden incapacitation**: pain that stops you from thinking and operating, vomiting, sweating and a drop in blood pressure, at a phase of flight no one chooses. Hiding a stone at the medical exposes the pilot to losing the **certificate**, facing an **investigation** and being left without **insurance**; under US rules, a pilot may not fly while knowing of a condition that makes them unfit. A passenger who boards with colic may have an **obstruction with infection**, which becomes an emergency on board, and may lose **travel insurance** cover.
**Remédios e voo.** O **anti-inflamatóri: **Medicines and flying.** An **anti-inflammatory** is the first medicine for colic and, for crew members, is accepted depending on the underlying condition. **Opioids**, such as morphine, codeine and tramadol, are **Do Not Fly** for the FAA: the pilot waits **5 half-lives** after the last dose. **Tamsulosin**, used to help the stone pass, is an alpha-blocker: it can cause **dizziness on standing**, and in the United Kingdom the pilot is grounded for at least **2 weeks** after starting or increasing the dose. Medicines to prevent new stones point to a **metabolic cause under treatment**, which under the FAA sends the case to the authority's decision.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** A prevençã: **How to prevent and ease it.** Prevention starts with water: **2.5 to 3 litres a day**, preferably water, so as to pass more than **2.5 litres** of urine; less **salt**, 4 to 5 g a day, animal protein in moderation and **normal calcium** in food, without cutting out milk. In flight, drink in sips before thirst and check that your urine is pale (See M2V14 - I). Anyone who has had a stone carries their **usual painkiller** in hand luggage and the urologist's report. Crew members keep their **imaging results** and the urologist's note for the examiner and do not fly with pain in the side, blood in the urine or fever.

Doença renal crônica, diálise e transpla: Chronic kidney disease, dialysis and transplant
Quem tem doença renal, faz diálise ou re: Can people with kidney disease, on dialysis or with a new kidney fly, and what changes for crew members?
Na **doença renal crônica**, o rim perde: In **chronic kidney disease**, the kidney gradually loses its ability to filter, over years, most often because of **diabetes** or **high blood pressure**. The loss is measured by the **estimated glomerular filtration rate** (eGFR), calculated from blood creatinine. The lower the eGFR, the more salt, water and waste the body retains, blood pressure rises and **erythropoietin** falls short, which brings **anaemia**. When the kidney almost stops, life depends on **dialysis** or a **transplant**.
No voo, o rim doente não piora por causa: In flight, the diseased kidney does not get worse because of altitude, but what comes with it matters. **Anaemia** adds to the cabin's low oxygen and brings tiredness and breathlessness (See M2V11 - II). People on dialysis usually have a **fluid limit** and gain water weight between sessions: hours of sitting make the **legs** swell. **High blood pressure** and a heart under more strain raise cardiovascular risk (See M2V2). In transplant recipients, the risk lies in **delaying the immunosuppressant** and in catching an **infection** with reduced defences.
O tratamento segue três caminhos. O **ex: Treatment follows three paths. **Expectant** management monitors eGFR, blood pressure, sugar and protein in the urine in the early stages. **Non-invasive** treatment uses medicines for blood pressure and to protect the kidney, corrects anaemia and, when needed, **peritoneal dialysis**, done at home with a fluid exchanged through the abdomen. **Invasive** treatment includes **haemodialysis**, which filters the blood in a machine, usually three times a week through a **fistula** in the arm, and **kidney transplantation**. The outlook improves greatly with early control, and a transplant gives almost everyone back a life that includes travel.
**Quando pode voar o passageiro.** A doe: **When passengers can fly.** Stable kidney disease does not prevent flying. People on dialysis plan the flight on **non-dialysis days** and **do not miss a session to travel**; the dialysis unit at the destination is booked in advance, usually **3 months** ahead for international travel. For peritoneal dialysis, fluid is delivered to the destination about **2 days before** arrival. Transplant recipients speak to their **transplant team before booking**, carry their medicines in hand luggage, with more than they need, and protect their skin from the sun.
**Quando pode voar o tripulante.** Na FA: **When crew members can fly.** Under the FAA, an eGFR of **45 to 59** without symptoms allows issue; **35 to 44** follows the **CACI**, except with a single kidney; **34 or less**, symptoms, a lot of protein in the urine or a single kidney with eGFR of 44 or less go to an **FAA decision**, as do **dialysis** and **transplant**; transplant recipients are assessed after **6 months** of recovery. Anaemia with haemoglobin below **10 g/dL** also defers issue. In Europe, dialysis makes the pilot unfit; creatinine clearance below **20 mL/min** is unacceptable; a transplant may be certified from **12 months**, in Class 1 with another pilot on board. Under **ANAC** rules, an applicant with kidney disease is assessed by kidney function, and a transplant recipient may be fit, in consultation with the agency, with no rejection and good tolerance of treatment.
**Voar sem liberação** tem custo para o: **Flying without clearance** costs the body and the career. Missing a dialysis session because of the trip builds up **potassium** and **fluid**, which can lead to arrhythmia and breathlessness on board. Delaying the immunosuppressant opens the way to **rejection** of the new kidney. A crew member who flies without reporting a fall in kidney function, dialysis or a transplant risks the **certificate**, an investigation and **insurance**. A passenger who travels without telling the airline and without a dialysis booking may be left without treatment at the destination.
**Remédios e voo.** Os remédios de **pre: **Medicines and flying.** **Blood-pressure** medicines are accepted for crew members within the authority's lists, without disruptive side effects (See M2V2 - II). Long-term **anti-inflammatories** should be avoided in kidney disease, because they reduce blood flow to the kidney. **Immunosuppressants** must be reported to the FAA, which asks for special attention to **calcineurin inhibitors**; in the United Kingdom, a transplant recipient's steroid dose must stay below **10 mg a day**. Transplant recipients follow the **timing leeway** agreed with their team: usually 2 to 3 hours, and up to 3 time zones without changing the medicine clock.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes do v: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before the flight, confirm **dialysis at the destination**, carry the **nephrologist's report**, the medicine list and the latest tests, and choose flights on non-dialysis days. During the flight, follow your nephrologist's **fluid limit** rather than drinking freely, walk and move your legs so the swelling does not get worse, and take the immunosuppressant at the agreed time. Transplant recipients prefer bottled water at the destination and protect their skin from the sun. Crew members keep their **eGFR**, haemoglobin and urine protein from the last **90 days** for the examiner.

Por que a próstata aumentada, a bexiga a: Why do an enlarged prostate, an urgent bladder and a urinary infection complicate flying, and which medicines can a pilot use?
A **próstata** fica logo abaixo da bexig: The **prostate** sits just below the bladder and wraps around the urethra. With age it grows: this is **benign prostatic hyperplasia** (BPH), which squeezes the urethra and leaves a weak stream, a bladder that does not empty properly and the urge to pass urine at night. An **overactive bladder**, in men and women, contracts without warning and brings **urgency** and leaks. A **urinary infection** may stay in the bladder, **cystitis**, with burning and frequent urges, or climb to the kidney, **pyelonephritis**, with **fever**, chills and back pain.
No voo, o problema é o **tempo sem banhe: In flight, the problem is **time without a toilet**. The seat-belt sign, the queue and the critical phase of flight force you to hold your urine. In BPH, an **over-full** bladder, **alcohol** and drowsy-making medicines, such as older antihistamines and some travel-sickness remedies, can make the urethra **lock**: **urinary retention** is very painful and is only relieved with a catheter, which may require a diversion. The urgency of an overactive bladder **distracts** the pilot, and pyelonephritis brings fever and dehydration that add to the dry air (See M2V14 - I).
O tratamento segue três caminhos. O **ex: Treatment follows three paths. **Expectant** management watches mild BPH and the bladder with changes in habits: less fluid at night, less caffeine and bladder training. **Non-invasive** treatment uses medicines: the **alpha-blocker**, which relaxes the prostate; the **5-alpha-reductase inhibitor**, which shrinks it over months; **antimuscarinics** and **beta-3 agonists** for an overactive bladder; and an **antibiotic** for infection. **Invasive** treatment includes **transurethral resection of the prostate** (TURP), laser and other techniques, and a **catheter** for retention. The outlook is good: most people control their symptoms and keep flying.
**Quando pode voar.** O **passageiro** c: **When you can fly.** A **passenger** with controlled BPH or overactive bladder flies normally, in an aisle seat. With **cystitis** without fever and an antibiotic started, they can usually fly, staying hydrated; with **fever**, chills or back pain, they do not fly until a doctor assesses them. Anyone with a **catheter** carries spare bags and empties the bag before boarding. For **crew members**, the FAA issues with **uncomplicated BPH**; under **ANAC** rules, genitourinary disease requires investigation with a urine test and a judgement that it does not affect flight; in Europe, **urological surgery** makes the pilot unfit until recovery is complete, with no symptoms.
Depois da **RTU de próstata**, o piloto: After **TURP**, the pilot returns when the surgeon clears them for **full activity**, and the surgery is reported at the next FAA medical. **Flying without clearance** has a price: urinary retention on board may require a catheter and a diversion; the fever of pyelonephritis may become a blood infection far from hospital; and a crew member who uses an unaccepted medicine or hides surgery risks the **certificate**, an investigation and **insurance**. A passenger with an infection and fever may be refused boarding and lose **travel insurance** cover.
**Remédios e voo.** O **alfabloqueador**: **Medicines and flying.** An **alpha-blocker** (tamsulosin, alfuzosin) can lower blood pressure on standing and cause dizziness and blurred vision: in the United Kingdom, the pilot is grounded for at least **2 weeks** after starting or increasing the dose, with three lying and standing blood-pressure readings; the FAA accepts it once the final dose is stable, without side effects. A **5-alpha-reductase inhibitor** (finasteride, dutasteride) requires **48 hours** in the United Kingdom and about **2 days** without side effects for the FAA. For an overactive bladder, the FAA puts **oxybutynin**, **tolterodine** and **solifenacin** on the **Do Not Issue** list; in the United Kingdom, bladder medicines require **4 weeks** on the ground and, in Class 1, another pilot on board for up to **4 months**.
O **antibiótico** da infecção urinária r: The **antibiotic** for a urinary infection clears cystitis in a few days, and what decides a crew member's flight is the illness: with fever, pain or feeling unwell, they do not fly; without symptoms and without side effects from the medicine, they return. **Drowsy antihistamines** and **opioids** stay out of flying: the FAA requires waiting **5 half-lives** after the last dose of a Do Not Fly medicine. An abnormal urine test at the medical calls for **investigation**, and any episode of **visible blood in the urine** is investigated (See M2V14 - V).
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes do v: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before the flight, go to the **toilet** before boarding and choose an **aisle seat**. During the flight, drink water in sips spread out over time, not large amounts at once, avoid **alcohol** and **drowsy antihistamines**, and do not hold your urine for hours: go to the toilet when the sign allows and before the descent. Anyone with a **catheter** empties the bag before boarding and carries spare bags. **Fever**, back pain or being unable to pass urine call for telling the crew. Crew members start a new prostate or bladder medicine **off the roster** and only return after the authority's waiting period.

O que fazer com sangue na urina, e quand: What should you do about blood in the urine, and when can you fly after cancer, kidney removal or other urological surgery?
**Sangue na urina**, ou **hematúria**, p: **Blood in the urine**, or **haematuria**, may be **visible**, turning the urine pink, red or tea-coloured, or show up only on a **dipstick** and under the microscope. Causes range from stones and infection to **tumours of the kidney, bladder and prostate**. That is why any episode of **visible** blood is treated as significant and investigated, and invisible blood counts as persistent when it appears on **2 out of 3 dipsticks**. Protein in the urine together with blood points to disease of the kidney's filter itself (See M2V14 - III).
No voo, o que pesa é o **pós-operatório*: In flight, what matters is the **post-operative period**. After keyhole surgery, **gas** left in the abdomen grows during the climb and causes pain and pressure (See M1V1 - II). Pelvic surgery and hours of sitting increase the risk of **thrombosis** (See M2V2 - VII). A **catheter** or **stent** requires an empty bag and a plan for the toilet. In cancer, **anaemia** and the fatigue of treatment add to the cabin's low oxygen (See M2V11 - III). Donating a kidney or removing a diseased one leaves a **single kidney**, which works well if it is healthy.
O tratamento segue três caminhos. O **ex: Treatment follows three paths. **Expectant** management is **active surveillance** of low-risk prostate cancer, with PSA and regular tests. **Non-invasive** treatment includes **radiotherapy**, **brachytherapy** (radioactive seeds in the prostate), chemotherapy and hormonal medicines. **Invasive** treatment includes **transurethral resection** of a bladder tumour, **nephrectomy** (removal of part or all of the kidney), **prostatectomy** and **cystectomy**, removal of the bladder. The outlook depends on the type and stage: tumours caught early, without metastasis, usually allow a return to flying.
**Quando pode voar o passageiro.** Depoi: **When passengers can fly.** After keyhole surgery, the advice is to avoid flying for about **24 hours**; after open abdominal surgery, for **10 days**. These periods apply to keyhole kidney removal, including donation, provided the surgeon clears you and there is no pain, fever or bleeding. With a **catheter**, passengers carry spare bags and empty the bag before boarding. During chemotherapy, anaemia and infections decide the flight (See M2V11 - III). Unexplained visible blood in the urine calls for a consultation **before** the trip.
**Quando pode voar o tripulante.** Na FA: **When crew members can fly.** Under the FAA, kidney and prostate cancer **without metastasis**, with treatment completed **5 or more years** ago and no recurrence, allow issue; **less than 5 years** ago, they follow the **CACI**; with **metastasis** or **recurrence**, they go to an FAA decision. In prostate cancer, the CACI accepts active surveillance or brachytherapy, with a **PSA** from the last 6 months of up to **20** without prostatectomy or up to **0.2** after it, no painkillers and release by the surgeon. In Europe, major urological surgery makes the pilot unfit until full recovery; a compensated **nephrectomy**, without high blood pressure, allows a return; a **cystectomy** with good urinary function, in Class 1, continues with another pilot on board; and anyone who **donated a kidney** and has normal function returns without restriction. Under **ANAC** rules, nephrectomy is accepted when the remaining kidney compensates well.
**Voar sem liberação** cobra caro. Voar: **Flying without clearance** has a high price. Flying the day after open surgery can reopen the wound, cause bleeding or bring on **thrombosis** far from help; ignoring visible blood in the urine can delay the diagnosis of a tumour. A crew member who flies during treatment or hides a recurrence risks the **certificate**, an investigation and **insurance**. A passenger who boards just after surgery without the surgeon's clearance may be refused boarding and lose **travel insurance** cover.
**Remédios e voo.** Depois da cirurgia,: **Medicines and flying.** After surgery, **opioids** are **Do Not Fly** for the FAA, with a wait of **5 half-lives**, and the prostate cancer CACI requires the pilot to be **off post-operative painkillers**. An **anticoagulant** used to prevent thrombosis after surgery has its own rules (See M2V11 - II). In chemotherapy and radiotherapy, active treatment must be **completed** before certification (See M2V11 - III). Prostate **brachytherapy** is accepted in the CACI. **Hormonal** medicines for prostate cancer go into the report sent to the FAA.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Nunca igno: **How to prevent and ease it.** Never ignore **visible blood** in the urine: see a doctor before flying. After surgery, respect the surgeon's timing and the minimums of **24 hours** after keyhole surgery and **10 days** after open surgery, walk in the aisle and move your calves (See M2V2 - VII). Carry the **surgery report**, the medicine list and, with a catheter, spare bags in hand luggage. Crew members keep their **PSA**, reports and the oncologist's or urologist's note from the last **90 days** and return only with the authority's clearance.

O que muda com a idade quando o corpo en: What changes with age when the body meets the cabin, and why is reserve the key word?
Envelhecer não é doença, mas tira **rese: Ageing is not a disease, but it takes away **reserve**: the heart, lungs, kidneys and brain keep working well at rest, yet there is less margin when the environment gets tough. The cabin gets tough in several ways at once: less oxygen, dry air, hours of sitting, time zones and broken sleep. For a 30-year-old, each factor is small; for a 70-year-old, they add up and show as tiredness, dizziness or confusion.
Com **menos oxigênio** a 8.000 ft, o pul: With **less oxygen** at 8,000 ft, older lungs and hearts compensate with less slack, especially when heart or lung disease is already present (See M2V1 and M2V2). With **dry air**, thirst becomes less sensitive with age and the kidney concentrates urine less: dehydration arrives sooner and without warning (See M2V14 - I). With **hours of sitting**, the risk of thrombosis is higher than average, and the bladder and prostate call for the toilet more often.
Os **sentidos** mudam devagar. A partir: The **senses** change slowly. From the early 40s, the lens loses its ability to focus up close, **presbyopia**, and night vision becomes slower (See M2V4). Hearing begins to lose the **high pitches**, **presbycusis**, and cabin noise hides the consonants of conversations and announcements (See M2V3 - IV). **Sleep** becomes lighter, and the body adjusts to time zones with more difficulty (See M2V8). **Bones** and muscles lose mass, and a fall in turbulence or on the aircraft stairs causes more harm.
Com a idade também aumentam os **remédio: With age, **medicines** also increase. Each may be safe on its own, but together they add up to drowsiness, dizziness on standing and confusion, and old-style **antihistamines** and **sedatives** used to sleep on the flight are the ones most often listed among those older people should avoid. The combination of medicines, dehydration and low oxygen explains many faints and falls on board. That is why the medicine list always travels in hand luggage (See M2V15 - V).
Para o **tripulante**, a idade muda o ca: For **crew members**, age changes the exam calendar and, in international commercial transport, the limit for flying. In a European study of more than **82,000** pilots, the share of unfitness caused by the **heart** rose from **8%** between 20 and 40 to **28%** between 61 and 65 and **48%** above 65. Attention and speed fell with age, but **reasoning** held up, and experience makes up for much of the rest (See M2V15 - III and IV).
O que pode acontecer a bordo, quando a r: What can happen on board when reserve runs out: **fainting** on standing after hours of sitting, a **fall** in the aisle, **confusion** at night in an unfamiliar place, breathlessness in someone who already has heart disease and **thrombosis** in the legs after a long flight. Almost all of this can be prevented with preparation, water, movement and the right medicines, which is why age alone does not stop anyone flying as a passenger.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes do v: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before the flight, see your doctor **4 to 6 weeks** before long trips, carry your **medicine list** and the doctor's letter and request **assistance** from the airline if needed. During the flight, drink **water even without thirst**, stand up slowly, sitting for a moment before getting to your feet, walk and move your calves, keep your reading **glasses** at hand and avoid sleeping pills that cause confusion. Afterwards, give your body a day or two more to adjust to the time zone.

Visão, audição e atenção com a idade: Vision, hearing and attention with age
Por que o piloto de 50 anos precisa ler: Why does a 50-year-old pilot need to read the panel at another distance, and what does age do to hearing and attention?
O **cristalino** é uma lente elástica qu: The **lens** is an elastic lens that changes shape to focus up close. Over the years, it stiffens and loses this **accommodation**: this is **presbyopia**, tired eyes, which usually appears from the early 40s. First, small print fails in low light; later, in daylight too. On the flight deck, the distance that matters most is not only that of the paper in your hand, but that of the **panel**, about an arm's length ahead.
A idade traz outras mudanças lentas. O c: Age brings other slow changes. The lens becomes cloudier, **cataract**, and scatters light: headlights at night dazzle more and contrast falls (See M2V4 - VII). Hearing loses the **high pitches** first, **presbycusis**, exactly where the consonants that tell one word from another on the radio lie (See M2V3 - IV). Processing **speed** and divided attention drop a little, while **reasoning** and experience hold up and often compensate.
O tratamento segue três caminhos. O **ex: Treatment follows three paths. **Expectant** management monitors vision and hearing at periodic exams, with the prescription reviewed when it changes. **Non-invasive** treatment uses reading **glasses**, multifocals or contact lenses, and a **hearing aid**. **Invasive** treatment is **cataract surgery**, which replaces the lens with an artificial one and has its own waiting period before flying again (See M2V4 - VIII). The outlook is very good: once corrected, presbyopia takes no one off flying.
**Quando pode voar.** O **passageiro** c: **When you can fly.** A **passenger** with presbyopia or hearing loss flies without restriction: they bring their glasses and hearing aid, and ask the crew to repeat announcements if needed. For **crew members**, the FAA requires near vision of **20/40** at **16 inches**, about 40 cm, in all classes and, from **age 50**, also intermediate vision of **20/40** at **32 inches**, about 80 cm, the distance of the panel, in Class 1 and Class 2, with or without glasses. Hearing must understand a **conversational voice at 6 feet**, about 2 m, or pass audiometry.
**Voar sem liberação** ou sem os óculos: **Flying without clearance** or without the right glasses has a high price: misreading a number on the panel, missing a digit of the radio frequency or not seeing traffic in the dark are silent errors, which do not hurt and so go unnoticed. When the certificate requires corrective lenses, flying without them means flying outside the certificate's conditions, with risk to **insurance** and in the **investigation** of an incident.
**Remédios e voo.** Com a idade, os remé: **Medicines and flying.** With age, the medicines that most impair attention are **old antihistamines**, **sedatives** and sleeping pills, which in older people increase confusion and falls; for crew members, those that cause drowsiness are **Do Not Fly** for the FAA, with a wait of **5 half-lives**. Glaucoma eye drops and hearing aids are compatible with flying when stable (See M2V4 - VII). A new medicine for memory or attention is assessed by the examiner before flying.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Revise o g: **How to prevent and ease it.** Have your glasses prescription checked when reading starts to fail, without waiting for the exam. Crew members always carry a **spare pair** and test reading the panel and charts under night lighting; the hearing aid goes with spare batteries. In flight, turn up the reading light, ask for anything you did not understand to be repeated and confirm frequencies and numbers with your colleague. Sleep well before flying: tired attention is the first to fail with age.

Por que o certificado médico do piloto v: Why does a pilot's medical certificate last less time after 40 and 60, and what is the ECG looking for?
O risco que mais cresce com a idade é o: The risk that grows most with age is that of the **heart**: plaques in the arteries, high blood pressure, arrhythmias and heart failure appear later in life and can cause **sudden incapacitation**, such as a heart attack or fainting at the controls (See M2V2). In the European pilot study, the heart accounted for **8%** of unfitness between 20 and 40, **13%** between 41 and 50, **21%** between 51 and 60, **28%** between 61 and 65 and **48%** above 65. That is why the exam calendar tightens with age.
O **eletrocardiograma** registra a eletr: The **electrocardiogram** records the heart's electricity and looks for signs of an **old heart attack**, arrhythmia and strain on the chambers, often before any symptom. Under the FAA, a Class 1 applicant has an ECG at the **first application after age 35** and **every year after 40**, with the test no more than **60 days** old. Blood pressure, cholesterol, sugar, weight and smoking complete the risk calculation, and an abnormal ECG leads to tests such as an exercise test (See M2V2 - III).
A **validade do certificado** encurta co: **Certificate validity** shortens with age. Under the FAA, an airline captain's Class 1 lasts **12 months** under age 40 and **6 months** from 40; for private flying, **60 months** under 40 and **24 months** from 40. In Europe, Class 1 lasts 12 months and drops to **6 months** above **60** and, from 40, for those flying single-pilot with passengers; Class 2 lasts 60 months under 40, 24 months from 40 to 49 and **12 months** from 50. ICAO also requires renewal every 6 months above 60 in commercial transport.
No Brasil, o **CMA** do piloto de linha: In Brazil, the **medical certificate** of airline, commercial and multi-crew pilots lasts **12 months** and drops to **6 months** from **40** in single-pilot commercial operations carrying passengers and from **60** in commercial transport. For private pilots, it lasts **60 months** before 40, **24 months** from 40 to 50 and **12 months** from 50. **Passengers** have no compulsory exam: those with heart disease talk to their cardiologist before the trip and, if needed, use the **MEDIF** (See M2V2).
**Voar sem liberação**, com o certificad: **Flying without clearance**, with an expired certificate or hiding a heart symptom, means flying without a valid certificate: the pilot answers to the authority, loses **insurance** cover and, in an accident, the **investigation** finds the overdue exam. For the body, the risk is the event the exam might have caught earlier: a heart attack or arrhythmia at the controls, far from hospital.
**Remédios e voo.** Com a idade, entram: **Medicines and flying.** With age come medicines for **blood pressure**, **cholesterol** and heart prevention. Most are accepted for crew members, provided there are no side effects and they are on the authority's lists: the FAA accepts many antihypertensives and statins, reported at the medical (See M2V2 - II). The care is with medicines that cause **dizziness on standing** or a drop in blood pressure, which are started off the roster, and with the sum of several medicines, reviewed by the doctor at each exam.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Cuide dos: **How to prevent and ease it.** Look after the factors the exam measures: **blood pressure**, cholesterol, sugar, weight, smoking and physical activity, controlled from early on. Note the certificate's expiry date and book the exam with time to spare, bringing the ECG, blood tests and reports within the required period. Chest pain, breathlessness on exertion, palpitations or fainting are reasons **not to fly** and to see a doctor before the next flight, without waiting for the exam.

Até que idade o piloto pode voar no tran: Up to what age can a pilot fly in commercial transport, and why does the rule change with the number of pilots on the flight deck?
O limite de idade existe por um motivo:: The age limit exists for a reason: the risk of **sudden incapacitation** grows over the years, mainly from the heart, and no one can predict exactly who will be taken ill. With **two pilots**, if one is taken ill, the other takes over; with **only one**, there is no one to take over. That is why ICAO separates the two situations: in **international commercial air transport**, a pilot may fly single-pilot until **60** and, in a crew with more than one pilot, until **65**.
Até 2014, a ICAO exigia que o piloto de: Until 2014, ICAO required a pilot aged 60 to 65 to fly with a colleague **under 60**. Amendment 172 to Annex 1, applicable since **13 November 2014**, removed this requirement, and the FAA dropped the **pairing** rule in 2015. In the United States, the **age 65** limit applies to airline pilots; in domestic business aviation and air taxi, the FAA sets no maximum age. Some countries, such as **New Zealand**, have filed a difference to the ICAO rule and decide by fitness, not age.
No **Brasil**, o RBAC 61 traz os limites: In **Brazil**, RBAC 61 sets the limits for **international public air transport**: the pilot in command until **60**, unless with a younger second pilot, and no duty in that transport after **65**. The text requiring the second pilot to be under 60 predates the ICAO change and must be checked in the amendment in force [check against the reference]. In Europe, the rules follow ICAO, and a 2019 European study recommended keeping age 65 with **additional health measures**.
**Quando pode voar.** Abaixo dos 60 anos: **When you can fly.** Under 60, age does not limit commercial flying; what counts is the medical certificate. From **60 to 65**, the pilot continues in international commercial transport **only in a crew with more than one pilot**, with the certificate renewed every **6 months**. After **65**, they leave international commercial transport, but may keep flying where the country's rules allow: private flying, instruction, general aviation and, in some countries, domestic operations. **Passengers** have no age limit.
**Voar fora do limite** é voar sem licen: **Flying beyond the limit** means flying without a valid licence for that operation: the operator loses its authorisation, insurance does not cover it and the country overflown may refuse the flight. A pilot over 65 only enters another country's airspace if that country **accepts** it; permission cannot be assumed. Age is nobody's fault, but hiding a symptom to keep flying is: the certificate depends on reporting any change in health to the examiner.
**Remédios e voo.** A idade não muda a l: **Medicines and flying.** Age does not change the list of accepted medicines, but it increases their number: blood pressure, cholesterol, prostate, sleep and pain add up their effects, and what was safe on its own may cause dizziness in combination. Each new medicine starts **off the roster**, with the authority's waiting period (See M2V14 - IV and M2V8 - VII), and the full list goes to every exam. A medicine that causes drowsiness remains **Do Not Fly**, with a wait of **5 half-lives**, at any age.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Planeje a: **How to prevent and ease it.** Plan your career with the calendar in hand: at **60**, the certificate becomes 6-monthly and single-pilot commercial flying ends; at **65**, international commercial transport ends. Keep your heart health, vision and hearing up to date to get there fit. Before flying to another country after 65, check whether it accepts pilots of that age. Experience remains valuable in instruction, flight safety and general aviation.

Que direitos e cuidados tem o passageiro: What rights and care does a passenger aged 60 or over have, and how can falls, thrombosis and confusion on board be avoided?
Não existe idade máxima para ser **passa: There is no maximum age for being a **passenger**: what decides the flight is health, not the year of birth. In Brazil, a person aged **60 or over** is a **passenger needing special assistance** (PNAE) and is entitled to **priority boarding**, help with boarding and disembarking, a wheelchair and an escort through the airport. Assistance is requested when buying the ticket or at least **48 hours** in advance.
Quando é preciso **acompanhante** ou **d: When a **companion** or **medical document** is needed, notice is at least **72 hours**. The airline may ask for a **MEDIF** from anyone who needs oxygen or a stretcher or has a condition that may require medical help on board, and replies within 48 hours. A companion is required for anyone who cannot understand the safety instructions or use the toilet alone; the airline provides one or charges up to **20%** of the fare for the companion chosen by the passenger. **Oxygen** on board is arranged with the airline at least **72 hours** before.
A bordo, os riscos do idoso são três. A: On board, older people face three risks. **Thrombosis**: the risk is higher than average and grows from **4 hours** of flight (See M2V2 - VII). **Falls**: weaker muscles, blood pressure that drops on standing, turbulence and drowsy medicine. **Confusion**: broken sleep, an unfamiliar place, dehydration and sedatives, especially in those who already have memory loss or dementia (See M2V6 - VII). All three are prevented with preparation, water, movement and the right medicines.
**Quando pode voar.** O idoso com doença: **When you can fly.** Older people with stable conditions fly normally, after a consultation **4 to 6 weeks** before long trips and with a **doctor's letter** listing their conditions, medicines by generic name, allergies and equipment. An unstable condition, such as breathlessness at rest, recent chest pain or new confusion, calls for assessment before buying the ticket. Frequent flyers with a stable condition can request a **FREMEC**, the frequent traveller's medical card.
**Voar sem preparo** cobra caro na idade: **Flying unprepared** has a high price with age: a fall in the aisle can break a hip, thrombosis can become an embolism days later and confusion at night can become a diversion. Travelling without telling the airline about oxygen or a companion can lead to **boarding being refused**, and travel insurance may not cover an undeclared pre-existing condition. **Insurance** with 24-hour assistance and medical evacuation is what best protects those travelling far.
**Remédios e voo.** Todos os remédios vã: **Medicines and flying.** All medicines go in **hand luggage**, in their original packaging, with extra for delays and a **written list**, with a copy in the suitcase too. Timing across time zones is agreed with the doctor (See M2V8 - IV). In older people, **old antihistamines** and **sedatives** used to sleep on the flight are among the medicines to avoid, because they increase confusion and falls. **Compression stockings** help prevent thrombosis on long flights, with the doctor's advice.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes, peç: **How to prevent and ease it.** Beforehand, request **assistance** when buying the ticket, prefer direct flights and an **aisle seat** near the toilet, and carry the doctor's letter. During the flight, drink **water even without thirst**, walk and move your calves, stand up slowly and hold the seat backs, keep your belt fastened when seated and do not take any sleeping pill other than your usual one. Afterwards, rest and allow an extra day for the time zone. Anyone with memory loss travels with a companion and with their name and address written down.

Por que existem classes de certificado m: Why are there classes of medical certificate, and what does each one protect in the body of those who fly?
O **Certificado Médico Aeronáutico**, o: The **Aeronautical Medical Certificate** attests that the body of someone who works in flight has enough reserve to do the job without falling into **incapacitation**. It can be **sudden**, when the heart fires an arrhythmia, the brain has a seizure or blood sugar plunges, or **subtle**, when attention, vision or reasoning fail without the person noticing. The examination looks in the body for exactly what can fail in the cockpit, and the class sets how strictly (See M2V2, M2V6 and M2V9).
No Brasil, o **RBAC 67** da ANAC divide: In Brazil, ANAC's **RBAC 67** divides the certificate into five classes. **Class 1** applies to airline transport, commercial and multi-crew pilots. **Class 2** applies to private pilots, flight attendants, flight engineers, balloon pilots and student pilots, except glider students. **Class 3** belongs to air traffic controllers, with rules outside ANAC. **Class 4** covers light-sport and glider pilots, and **Class 5**, remote pilots.
A **ICAO**, no Anexo 1, usa três classes: **ICAO**, in Annex 1, uses three classes. **Class 1** applies to commercial, multi-crew and airline transport licences; **Class 2**, to private, glider and balloon pilots, flight navigators and flight engineers; **Class 3**, to air traffic controllers and remote pilots. Flight attendants have no class in Annex 1: Brazil placed them in Class 2. The logic is the same in both systems: the more people depend on the body of the person flying, the stricter the examination (See M3V1 - II).
Strictness shows above all in the **validity period**. At ANAC, the Class 1 certificate is valid for **12 months** and drops to **6 months** from age 40 in single-pilot operations carrying passengers and from age 60 in public air transport. The private pilot's is valid for **60 months** before 40, **24 months** from 40 to 49 and **12 months** from 50. The flight attendant's is valid for 60 months before 60 and 24 months after, and the remote pilot's, 48 months. The examiner or ANAC may shorten any period when the clinical case calls for it (See M2V15 - III).
O prazo encurta com a idade porque o ris: The period shortens with age because the body's risk changes. Arteries build up plaque, the heart rhythm becomes more prone to failure, blood pressure rises and blood sugar slips out of control more often, and the heart is the cause of unfitness that grows most after 50 (See M2V15 - I). At any age, the **mind**, **sleep** and the use of **medicines and alcohol** also weigh in; they do not show on a routine examination and depend on an honest conversation with the examiner (See M2V7 and M2V8).
O exame segue o organismo de cima a baix: The examination follows the body from top to bottom: history, heart with an **electrocardiogram** at the set ages, blood pressure, lungs, distance, near and colour **vision**, **hearing**, nervous system, mind, urine and, when indicated, blood tests. Each part answers a practical question: does this body see the panel, hear the radio, reason under stress and stay stable for the whole duty period? Someone who needs lenses, for example, receives the **limitation** of flying with them and with a spare pair (See M2V4).
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes do e: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before the examination, crew members book the appointment well ahead of expiry, bring their reports and medicine list and declare everything that has changed since the last examination. Between examinations, the international rule is not to fly when aware of a **decrease in medical fitness** and to see the examiner after surgery, hospital admission, a new regular medicine or pregnancy (See M3V1 - II). Passengers do not need a certificate: their decision to fly goes through their own doctor and, when the airline asks, the medical form (MEDIF).

Se o corpo humano é o mesmo em todo luga: If the human body is the same everywhere, why does each country have its own rule, and what do they all share?
A **ICAO**, agência da ONU criada pela C: **ICAO**, the UN agency created by the Chicago Convention, publishes in **Annex 1** the minimum standards for licensing and medical examination. Each State writes its own rule from them: in Brazil, ANAC's **RBAC 67**; in the United States, the FAA's **14 CFR Part 67**; in Europe, EASA's **Part-MED**. Physiology is the same, but countries measure risk in different ways, and crew members who work abroad need to know the rule of the authority that issued their licence.
O Anexo 1 fixa a **validade** contada da: Annex 1 sets **validity** counted from the date of the examination: **12 months** for commercial, multi-crew and airline transport licences, **60 months** for private, glider and balloon pilots and **48 months** for controllers and remote pilots. With age, the periods shorten: **6 months** from 40 for commercial pilots carrying passengers alone and from 60 in commercial air transport, and **24 months** for private pilots, controllers and remote pilots after 40. Annex 1 also asks States to apply **safety management** to medical assessment, analysing in-flight incapacitation events, and to promote the health of those who fly.
A **FAA** usa três classes: a **1ª** par: The **FAA** uses three classes: **1st** for airline captains, **2nd** for commercial pilots and **3rd** for private and student pilots. The 1st class is valid for 12 months before age 40 and 6 months after, for airline transport privileges; the 2nd, 12 months; the 3rd, 60 months before 40 and 24 months after. For private flying there is also **BasicMed**: anyone who has held a certificate after July 2006 may fly aircraft of up to 12,500 lb, about 5,670 kg, with up to 7 occupants, 18,000 ft and 250 knots, taking a course every 24 months and an examination with their own doctor every 48 months, without pay and only in the United States, Mexico and the Bahamas.
Na Europa, a **Classe 1** vale para as l: In Europe, **Class 1** applies to commercial, multi-crew and airline transport licences, **Class 2** to private pilots and the **LAPL** to light aircraft. The initial Class 1 examination can only be done at an **aeromedical centre**, the AeMC. After the 2015 accident in the Alps, in which the co-pilot flew the aircraft into the mountains, Europe began requiring airlines to provide **peer support**, a **psychological assessment** before starting line flying and **alcohol testing**, rules in force since February 2021 (See M2V7).
Quando o corpo não atende ao padrão, as: When the body does not meet the standard, the rules do not shut the door at once. Annex 1 allows the certificate to be issued if an **accredited medical conclusion** shows that safety is not compromised, with the necessary limitations. The FAA has **special issuance**, with periodic reports from the treating doctor, and the **SODA**, for defects that do not change, such as the loss of an eye, after the pilot demonstrates safe flying. Europe uses **limitations**, such as flying only with another qualified pilot. In Brazil, ANAC rules on appeals against the examiner's decision.
Entre um exame e outro, a responsabilida: Between examinations, responsibility lies with the person who flies. Annex 1 forbids exercising the licence when holders are aware of a **decrease in medical fitness** that could compromise safety. The FAA forbids flying while knowing of a condition that would prevent certification or while using medicine that causes it. Europe lists when to see the examiner **without undue delay**: surgery or an invasive procedure, starting a regular medicine, significant injury or illness, pregnancy, hospital admission and the first need for lenses. Flying while hiding the condition puts the body at risk on board and may cost the licence, the insurance and the career.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes de t: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before working or flying under another authority, crew members check which medical certificate it requires and for how long it is valid, and keep copies of their reports and certificates. Anyone with special issuance or a limitation submits the follow-up reports and tests on time, because the certificate depends on them. After surgery, hospital admission, a new medicine or pregnancy, they see the examiner before returning to flying, not afterwards. The examiner explains each limitation in writing and what changes if the condition worsens.

Quem pode examinar o tripulante, e o que: Who may examine crew members, and what does the examiner look for in the body beyond what the crew member reports?
O **médico examinador** é o médico autor: The **medical examiner** is the doctor authorised by the authority to carry out the examination and to issue, deny or defer the certificate. In Brazil, RBAC 67 provides for the **accredited doctor**, who examines Classes 2, 4 and 5; the **registered doctor**, for Class 4 only; the **accredited clinic**, which examines any class under the responsibility of its medical technical director; and **partner entities**. **Class 1**, therefore, can only be done at an accredited clinic, a partner entity or ANAC itself, which also rules on appeals.
Nos Estados Unidos, o **AME** é designad: In the United States, the **AME** is designated by the FAA and, faced with a finding, may **issue**, **deny** or **defer** the certificate, sending the case to the FAA's medical division. For several stable conditions, after the FAA's first authorisation, the AME may renew the special issuance by following a protocol, the **AASI**. In Europe, the examination is done by the **AME** or the **aeromedical centre**, and Class 1 cases that do not meet the standard go to the authority. In all of them, the examiner answers for safety, not for treatment: that stays with the treating doctor.
O exame começa pela **história**: o trip: The examination begins with the **history**: the crew member signs a statement of their personal, family and hereditary history, required by Annex 1. That is where the mechanisms no machine shows come to light: the faint months ago, chest pain when climbing stairs, the sleeping pill, alcohol use, the sadness that does not lift. In the United States, a false statement on the form is a federal crime. In any country, it takes away the examiner's chance to protect the body of the person who will fly.
Depois vem o corpo. O examinador mede pr: Then comes the body. The examiner measures blood pressure and pulse, listens to the heart and lungs, examines distance, near and colour **vision**, **hearing**, balance and reflexes, and orders the **electrocardiogram** and blood and urine tests according to class and age (See M2V15 - III). They look for two things: disease that may cause **sudden incapacitation**, such as arrhythmia, heart attack, seizure or hypoglycaemia, and disease that may cause **subtle incapacitation**, such as depression, poor sleep, medicine side effects or declining attention.
O maior obstáculo não está no aparelho,: The biggest obstacle is not in the machine but in **fear**. In a survey of more than **3,500** US pilots, **56%** said they had avoided seeking medical care for fear of losing their certificate. Those who hide symptoms delay the diagnosis of treatable diseases, such as hypertension, sleep apnoea and depression, which worsen without care and reach the cockpit at a more serious stage. The examiner who listens, explains the options and keeps the statement confidential protects more than one who only stamps the form (See M2V7).
Erros dos dois lados custam caro. O trip: Mistakes on either side are costly. A crew member who flies with a hidden condition risks fainting, arrhythmia or a wrong decision at the controls, besides losing the licence and insurance cover and, after an accident, facing the investigation. An examiner who misses a finding or issues outside the rules may lose the designation and answer to the authority and the medical council. That is why, when in doubt, the examiner **defers** and asks for reports instead of deciding alone.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** O tripulan: **How to prevent and ease it.** Crew members choose their examiner in advance, bring the treating doctor's reports with diagnosis, treatment, doses and how long they have been stable, and declare everything, including over-the-counter medicines. They ask what each limitation means and what would lift it. The treating doctor writes the report with the flying role in mind, and the examiner explains the decision, records the limitations and, when in doubt, defers the certificate and asks for the missing information instead of denying or issuing in a hurry.

Quanto risco de incapacitação súbita a a: How much risk of sudden incapacitation does aviation accept in a pilot, and where does the 1% figure come from?
A **regra do 1%** nasceu no começo dos a: The **1% rule** was born in the early 1980s, at aviation cardiology meetings, to decide which pilots with heart disease could fly. The idea was to treat the pilot's body as any critical aircraft system is treated, which must cause a catastrophic failure less than **once every 1 billion hours** of flight. The same target came to apply to fatal accidents with a medical cause.
A conta segue o voo. As fases críticas,: The calculation follows the flight. The critical phases, **take-off and landing**, take up about **10%** of flight time. If a pilot becomes incapacitated in one of them, in a **two-pilot** operation, the other takes over, and only about **1 in 100** of these incapacitations ends in an accident; in a simulator study, it was 1 in 400. Together, the critical phase and the second pilot cut the risk a thousandfold. To reach 1 accident in 1 billion hours, each pilot may have up to **1 incapacitation in 1 million hours**, which, over 8,760 hours a year, comes to about **1% per year**.
No corpo, **incapacitação súbita** é qua: In the body, **sudden incapacitation** is any failure that suddenly takes the pilot away from the controls: arrhythmia, heart attack, fainting, seizure, stroke, hypoglycaemia or severe renal colic. In a study of more than **16,000** UK Class 1 pilots, the annual incapacitation rate was **0.25%**, rising from about **0.1%** between 20 and 39 to **0.42%** between 50 and 59 and **1.2%** between 60 and 69. Among incapacitations in flight, **psychiatric** causes were more typical than cardiac ones (See M2V7 and M2V14 - II).
A regra vale para o voo com **dois pilot: The rule applies to **two-pilot** flying. In single-pilot flying there is no one to take over, and the same risk weighs far more; in private flying, fewer people are exposed and the rule is more flexible. The New Zealand authority itself points out that 1% **is not a fixed rule**: in practice, with an annual risk below 1% the certificate is issued without limitation; from 1% to under 2%, with a limitation in Class 1 and without one in Class 2; from 2% to under 4%, only Class 2 is likely; above 4% to 5%, no certificate is likely.
A restrição mais usada para manter algué: The limitation most used to keep someone flying with a risk slightly above the limit is to fly **only with another qualified pilot**. It uses the same reasoning as the calculation: if the first pilot fails, the second takes over, and the risk that reaches the passenger falls a hundredfold. That is why a pilot with a treated, stable and monitored condition can keep flying, as long as never alone at the controls, while treatment and follow-up tests show the risk has not risen (See M3V1 - II).
O número tem limites. Ele depende de est: The figure has limits. It depends on estimating each person's risk, and risk calculators were built for the general population: in New Zealand, screening based on them missed more than half of the pilots who had an event. The calculation also captures **subtle incapacitation** poorly, such as fatigue, medicine effects and mental illness, which do not switch the pilot off at once but worsen decision-making. That is why aerospace medicine began to seek each person's own risk (See M3V1 - V).
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** O piloto r: **How to prevent and ease it.** Pilots lower their own risk by controlling what weighs most on the heart and brain: blood pressure, cholesterol, sugar, weight, smoking, alcohol and sleep, and they do not fly ill, tired or on a new medicine without advice. They have their follow-up tests on time, because proven stability is what sustains the certificate. The examiner estimates the annual risk with published data, records the reasoning and, when the risk is slightly over the limit, considers the limitation of flying with another pilot before denying.

A **medicina de precisão** troca a pergu: **Precision medicine** swaps the question "does this pilot meet the standard?" for "what is the risk in this body, and what lowers it?". It uses each person's history, family, tests and course over time to decide who needs further investigation, who can fly with a limitation and who can fly with none. Annex 1 itself asks States to analyse in-flight incapacitation events, reassess the rules with those data and promote the health of those who fly (See M3V1 - II).
O alvo mais estudado é o **coração**. A: The most studied target is the **heart**. Coronary disease grows silently for years, and the first sign may be a heart attack or sudden death, with no previous pain. Plaque of fat and calcium narrows the artery or ruptures, forms a clot and cuts blood to the heart muscle, which can lose its rhythm within minutes. A NATO group proposed screening crew in **three phases**: a risk calculator and resting electrocardiogram for everyone; imaging for those at increased risk; and ischaemia testing and catheterisation for those at high risk (See M2V2).
O **escore de cálcio** é uma tomografia: The **calcium score** is a quick CT scan that measures calcium in the coronary arteries. Zero means very low risk, with mortality below 0.1% per year, but it does not rule out non-calcified plaque. Above **100**, events exceed **1% per year**, and the group recommends removing crew members from duty until the investigation is complete. From **400**, catheterisation is considered. **CT coronary angiography** shows the channel of the artery, and narrowing above **50%** is a reasonable threshold to ground and investigate. Radiation is low: about 0.5 to 1 mSv for the score and 2 to 4 mSv for the angiography.
Nem todo exame serve para isso. O **test: Not every test serves this purpose. The **exercise test** alone has a sensitivity of only 60% to 70% for coronary disease and predicts events poorly, so it should not be used as the only test, although it remains useful to measure fitness and the blood-pressure response. **Ischaemia** tests come after imaging, as second line. A normal perfusion scan works as a "warranty": the risk of a significant event stays below **1% per year** for about **3 years** (See M3V1 - IV).
A outra frente é a **mente**. Depois do: The other front is the **mind**. After the 2015 accident in the Alps, Europe began requiring **peer support**, in which trained pilots confidentially support colleagues in distress, as well as a psychological assessment before line flying and alcohol testing. Precision here means finding early who needs help and treating without punishing, because a pilot who fears losing the licence hides the symptom, and it is untreated illness that reaches the cockpit as a danger (See M2V7 and M3V1 - III).
Mais exame também tem preço para o corpo: More testing also has a cost for the body and the career. Radiation adds up over the years, unimportant findings lead to more tests, and a false positive can take someone off flying for no reason. That is why screening is guided by risk rather than done the same way for everyone. Health data require confidentiality, and the result serves the crew member's health first: plaque found early is treated with medicine, physical activity and control of risk factors, and treatment may allow a return to flying.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** O tripulan: **How to prevent and ease it.** Crew members know their own risk: they ask the examiner about blood pressure, cholesterol, sugar and family history, and treat early whatever appears. They turn to peer support or a doctor at the first sign of distress, without waiting for a crisis. The examiner uses phased screening, chooses the test by the question to be answered, explains the radiation and the risk of unimportant findings and grounds only for the duration of the investigation, with a return plan.
